faqs.question: What are the five topic areas in IB mathematics?
faqs.answer: Number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, and calculus. Both Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation use the same five headings and weight them very differently: Analysis and Approaches concentrates on algebra, functions and calculus, while Applications and Interpretation concentrates on statistics, probability and modelling. Every examination question belongs to one of the five, which is what makes a precise diagnosis possible from a marked paper rather than a general verdict about mathematical ability.

faqs.question: Why does my child lose marks on the non-calculator paper specifically?
faqs.answer: Because hand fluency decays silently over two years of graphing-display use, and the paper examines a finite list of hand skills: exact trigonometric values, surds, index and logarithmic laws, completing the square, differentiation by rule, definite integration and sketching from an equation. None of it is conceptually difficult and most of it has not been practised by hand since Year 11. The diagnostic is quick and uncomfortable: take the device out of the room and set twenty minutes of questions from that list.

faqs.question: What does 'show that' mean in an IB maths question?
faqs.answer: That the answer is given to you and the marks are entirely in the working. A student who writes the stated result and nothing else scores zero on a question they could have done completely. It is one of several mathematical command terms that behave differently from other subjects': 'hence' obliges you to use the previous part, 'hence or otherwise' releases that, 'write down' signals no working is expected, and 'verify' means substitute and confirm rather than solve. Two or three sessions covers all of them.

faqs.question: Why can't my child prepare for Higher Level Paper 3 with normal revision?
faqs.answer: Because Papers 1 and 2 reward recognising a question type and executing a known method, while Paper 3 rewards holding an argument together across eight or ten connected parts in an unfamiliar context. A student who is excellent at short questions can be genuinely lost, and the loss is not about knowledge. What works is practising whole questions, and learning to move past a difficult middle part and return, because many later marks are reachable from the earlier results alone.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a maths tutor to Tilal Al Ghaf?
faqs.answer: No. All UAE tuition is delivered live and one-to-one over video, scheduled to Gulf Standard Time, and home visits are a service we run only in India. For mathematics the format costs almost nothing, because a session is worked problems on a shared screen with the student's own working visible line by line, and a paper marked in front of them. What it gains is a shortlist of tutors who teach your child's exact course rather than those willing to drive out past Hessa Street on a weekday.

faqs.question: How should a Diploma maths student use past papers?
faqs.answer: Four elements, and most students use one. Work non-calculator questions with the device out of the room, or the practice is worthless for the paper it was meant to prepare. Time the work, because pacing is where a large share of marks go. Mark against the published scheme rather than against whether the answer looks right. And tag every lost mark with a topic and a loss type, keeping the tally across several papers. The tally is the point: after three or four papers a pattern appears that no single paper shows.

faqs.question: Which calculator mistakes cost marks on the permitted papers?
faqs.answer: Two opposite ones. Under-use, where a student labours by hand through a question the device was meant to answer and then does not finish the paper — which gets misdiagnosed as a content problem. And over-reliance without method, where a displayed answer appears with no supporting working, forfeiting method marks. In statistics the dominant version is a correct regression equation or test statistic with no sentence saying what it means in the context of the data, which is where the marks actually were.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a non-calculator block take?
faqs.answer: Four to six sessions plus set work, and it is among the highest-yield blocks in Diploma mathematics because the marks are spread across a whole paper rather than concentrated in one topic. The usual stalling points are exact trigonometric values and logarithmic manipulation, each of which takes one or two sessions. A student who recovers hand fluency does not gain marks in one area; they stop leaking them everywhere on a paper carrying a substantial share of the grade.

faqs.question: What makes a good exploration topic?
faqs.answer: One the student can genuinely investigate using mathematics at or slightly beyond their course level, with a real reason for having chosen it. Use of mathematics is the largest of the five criteria in a total of twenty marks, so a safe topic using simple mathematics cannot reach the upper bands however well it is presented. A question that is too large produces description instead of mathematics. Testing viability takes an hour of conversation and saves a term of writing in the wrong direction.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE preparation suits Diploma mathematics best?
faqs.answer: Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606 or Pearson Further Pure Mathematics 4PM1 taken alongside the main course, because both introduce calculus, logarithms and trigonometric identities before the Diploma does. In this part of Dubailand, where provision is predominantly British curriculum, most Diploma mathematics students arrive via IGCSE, and whether they took one of those is the best single predictor of their first term. The Extended or Higher tier in the main course is effectively a prerequisite in any case.

faqs.question: What should a maths tutoring block cost and how long should it be?
faqs.answer: Read it as blocks rather than months. A non-calculator restoration block is four to six sessions, command terms two to three, calculator technique two, exploration coaching six to eight across a term, and whole-topic repair a holiday block of four or five sessions a week. At the qualified subject tutor band of AED 150 to AED 300 an hour read in October 2026, each has a calculable price and a named target. Open-ended weekly support with no target is the most expensive thing in this market.

faqs.question: Is an early weekday session really better for maths?
faqs.answer: For whole papers, yes, and this community makes it possible. A Higher Level paper runs two hours and has to be sat intact at least sometimes, because accuracy falls in the final half hour and that is where a grade goes. A paper attempted at seven in the evening after a school day and other homework tests tiredness rather than mathematics and produces a misleadingly poor result. Tilal Al Ghaf pupils are often home before four, so a weekday block is feasible rather than weekend-only.

faqs.question: My child's statistics answers are numerically right but score low. Why?
faqs.answer: Because in Applications and Interpretation particularly, the marks are attached to the interpretation rather than to the number. A correct regression equation, correlation coefficient or test statistic with no sentence explaining what it means for the data in the question earns very little, and a hypothesis test with no conclusion referring back to the hypotheses earns less still. The fix is a habit rather than knowledge: write the context sentence every time, with a templated structure for test conclusions until it becomes automatic.

faqs.question: Can a tutor work on the mathematics an exploration needs?
faqs.answer: Yes, including content beyond the course if the student's chosen question requires it, and that is a legitimate and valuable use of a tutor. A tutor can also test whether a topic is viable, explain each criterion and its descriptors, and give feedback on the student's own drafts. What a tutor cannot do is write any part of it, supply the mathematics as a finished solution to be transcribed, or choose the topic outright, because personal engagement and reflection reward thinking the student actually did.

faqs.question: Do maths tutors in the UAE need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years, covering registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without it is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, although no fine schedule is published, so be sceptical of quoted amounts. Ask to see the permit rather than accepting a verbal assurance, and ask any agency the same.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-tilal-al-ghaf.closingBody: Mathematics is the Diploma subject where you can find out precisely what is wrong, so insist on precision. Three or four papers tagged that way produce a pattern that is almost always narrower than the student believed, and that pattern names the block: non-calculator restoration, command terms, calculator technique, exploration coaching or whole-topic repair. Then take the early slot this community allows and spend it on a whole paper. Tilal Al Ghaf sessions run live and one-to-one over video at Gulf Standard Time. We make no home visits in the UAE and promise no grades.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-town-square.tutorsIntro: Maths tutors matched to Town Square students hold a fixed weekly slot built round the school run, and teach one of the four IB routes rather than general secondary mathematics.

intro.heading: When can a maths session actually happen in a Town Square week?
paragraphs: Maths is the subject families book at the wrong hour more often than any other, because it is the one they worry about most and so they take whatever slot is offered. That is a worse mistake in maths than elsewhere. A tired student can read a history chapter and retain something. A tired student cannot follow a calculus derivation, cannot hold three variables in mind while rearranging an expression, and cannot concentrate through the twenty minutes of silent working that a past-paper question actually requires.

The Town Square timetable makes the point sharply. Town Square is a Nshama community off Al Qudra Road, and the schools running IB Diploma maths are not next door — most Diploma students here travel to Motor City, Dubai Sports City, or further into Al Barsha and Silicon Oasis. A school day ending at half three becomes a 4:45pm arrival home once the afternoon traffic is counted, and from an inner-city school it is closer to five.

Now add a tutor who must drive to you. They are leaving another part of Dubai in the same traffic, so a six o'clock start is optimistic and half six is realistic. The session then runs to eight, with a student who has been awake and working for thirteen hours, on the single most attention-expensive subject in their timetable. The arrangement is not failing because the tutor is weak. It is failing because the hour is wrong, and in a community this far out the hour is the scarce resource.

IB Gram removes travel from both ends. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and we make no home visits anywhere in the UAE — in-home tutoring is a service we run in India only. A session can therefore start at 4:45pm for a Year 12 student, or at 8pm for a Year 13 student who works late anyway and is sharpest once the house is quiet. Both are better hours than any visiting arrangement can offer from Al Qudra Road.

The second thing to establish before anything else is which course your child sits. The IB runs two mathematics courses at two levels: Analysis and Approaches, the algebraic and proof-oriented route, and Applications and Interpretation, the modelling and statistics route, each at Higher and Standard Level. They are not harder and easier versions of one thing. A tutor matched to the wrong one teaches correct mathematics in proportions the paper will not reward.

The rest of this page is built from those two facts: the four windows in a Town Square week and what each supports, the Diploma maths year term by term so you can see when help is worth most, and the published AED rates with every figure attributed.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-town-square.programmesIntro: The right hour and the right help both change with the stage. These are the IB maths stages we cover for Town Square families.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme mathematics
programmes.description: Mathematics inside units of inquiry, assessed continuously by the class teacher. Number sense, pattern, measurement and the ability to explain a method in words are the real outputs, and a child who can compute but not explain looks weaker here than their arithmetic warrants.
programmes.countryNote: Primary children on a long Town Square school run are tired by four o'clock, and a session after five is usually wasted money whatever the subject. For this age group the workable options are immediately off the run or a weekend morning, and we would rather say that than sell an evening slot destined to fail.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme mathematics
programmes.description: Four criteria on a 0-8 scale: knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Criterion B rewards generalising from a pattern and justifying it, which no traditional maths lesson drills, and criterion C marks the quality of communication rather than the answer.
programmes.countryNote: MYP students sustain a 5pm or 5:30pm session comfortably, which is the band most Town Square families settle into. The criterion profile is also the best available signal about the eventual AA or AI choice, and almost nobody reads it that way.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme mathematics
programmes.description: Analysis and Approaches emphasises algebraic methods, proof and calculus; Applications and Interpretation emphasises modelling, statistics and the use of technology. Both carry an Exploration worth 20% of the grade, and Higher Level adds a third written paper plus substantially more content in both courses.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students are the group that can genuinely use an 8pm slot and often prefer it. They are also the group for whom a visiting tutor's half six arrival does the most damage, because early evening is their most productive independent hour and it gets spent waiting at the window.

programmes.name: The IGCSE or MYP to Diploma maths bridge
programmes.description: The largest step in IB mathematics. A student arriving from IGCSE Extended or MYP maths into Analysis and Approaches Higher Level meets a jump in algebraic demand, abstraction and pace inside the first term. Comfortable at sixteen does not predict comfortable in November of Year 12.
programmes.countryNote: The best-value intervention in the whole sequence, and the one with the least urgency attached to it. A short summer block on algebraic fluency, functions and trigonometric identities costs a fraction of the Year 13 rescue it prevents, and the summer is also the only period when a Town Square week has spare hours in it.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-town-square.subjectsIntro: The IB mathematics routes and components Town Square students need, with the specific place marks go in each. Availability varies by level and term and is confirmed at the trial lesson.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL
subjects.description: The most demanding IB maths route. Proof by induction and contradiction, complex numbers, vectors and calculus well beyond Standard Level, plus a third paper rewarding sustained reasoning. Small algebraic weaknesses surface within a term rather than a year.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches SL
subjects.description: Algebra, functions, trigonometry, calculus and probability without the HL extensions. Marks go on calculus application questions and on the unstructured parts of the calculator paper where nothing indicates which technique is wanted.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation HL
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics taken seriously, plus matrices, graph theory and complex numbers — genuinely surprising to anyone who chose AI expecting less abstraction. The third paper demands extended modelling with technology.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation SL
subjects.description: Modelling, descriptive and inferential statistics, financial mathematics and fluent calculator use. The usual failure is choosing it as the lighter option and meeting regression and hypothesis testing with no statistical language to think in.

subjects.name: The Exploration
subjects.description: Worth 20% of the final grade in every IB maths course, assessed on presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics. Difficulty is not on that list, which catches strong students out.

subjects.name: Calculus
subjects.description: Differentiation and integration techniques, kinematics, related rates and at HL differential equations. Students can usually differentiate and struggle to recognise which technique a worded problem calls for, which is pattern recognition rather than knowledge.

subjects.name: Statistics and probability
subjects.description: Distributions, correlation, regression and hypothesis testing. Marks sit in interpretation: a student who produces a p-value and cannot say what it means about the claim loses most of the credit available on the question.

subjects.name: Proof and algebraic technique
subjects.description: Induction, contradiction, manipulation of rational and surd expressions, binomial expansion and identities. The foundation layer, and where almost every struggling Year 13 AA student actually needs work rather than in the topic they name.

subjects.name: Graphical calculator technique
subjects.description: Both courses assume fluent use of the permitted technology, and marks are lost daily on avoidable things: wrong window settings, not stating the model fitted, or working by hand what the calculator was provided for.

subjects.name: MYP mathematics criteria work
subjects.description: Criterion-by-criterion support against knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. The only honest preparation for either Diploma route, and a useful signal about which one.

subjects.name: IGCSE and Additional Mathematics bridging
subjects.description: A short targeted block on the algebra, functions and trigonometry that Analysis and Approaches assumes and IGCSE does not fully build. Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606 covers some of it; students who skipped it arrive with a visible gap.

sections.heading: Four windows in a Town Square week, and what maths each supports
paragraphs: Scheduling ends more tutoring arrangements than teaching does. A family agrees a time that works in September, then football moves to Tuesdays, an Exploration deadline lands in November, and by February the sessions have stopped without anybody deciding to stop them. Choosing the window properly at the start is worth more than any amount of rescue later.

There are four candidate windows out here. Straight off the school run, 4:30pm to 5:30pm, which only exists if nobody is travelling to you. After dinner from seven, which competes directly with the student's own best independent working hour. Late, from eight, which Diploma students use well and younger students cannot. And weekend mornings, which are the most reliable and the least booked.

For maths specifically the ranking is clearer than for other subjects, because the subject's demands differ by task. New teaching — a technique the student has not met, a derivation, a proof method — needs the alert window and should go early. Consolidation and worked practice tolerate the later slot. Exploration work wants a long uninterrupted block, which in practice means a weekend. Timed past-paper practice with marking wants ninety minutes, which rules out the sixty-minute after-dinner slot.

Decide it with your child in the room, because they know which hour they can think in better than either of us does. Then protect it, and plan the Ramadan change deliberately rather than discovering it: shortened school days, evenings reorganised around Iftar, and a shift to a late-morning, early-afternoon or post-Iftar slot, or a deliberate pause with a heavier block afterwards.

sections.heading: The Diploma maths year, term by term
paragraphs: Knowing when help is worth most is as useful as knowing what kind of help it is, and for maths the answer is weighted heavily towards the start. Everything in the course sits on algebraic fluency, the Exploration is finished long before exam revision begins, and paper technique is the only lever still available in the final term.

Term by term, it runs roughly like this. End of Year 11: course and level chosen, against the intended degree rather than against current comfort. First term of Year 12: new content begins and any algebraic weakness is exposed — this is the cheapest and most effective point to intervene. Second and third terms of Year 12: content builds, and the Exploration topic should be chosen in this window while it can still be a good topic rather than an available one.

First term of Year 13: remaining content, Exploration drafted and finished to the school's internal deadline, then mocks. Second term: paper technique, including dedicated work on the third paper for Higher Level candidates, which most schools reach late because practice naturally concentrates on the papers both levels sit. Then the May session.

One honesty note that belongs in any calendar section. The IB's own site blocks automated retrieval, so no IB exam or results date in this project has been confirmed from ibo.org. We name the May session as the one UAE schools sit and publish no specific date; get those from your school's IB coordinator or ibo.org. Cambridge and Pearson dates are published and we use them: Cambridge runs June and November series with the February/March series offered to India only, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November.

sections.heading: Which course is your child on, and why it decides the match
paragraphs: Before any scheduling matters, establish the route. The IB runs Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches and Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation, each at Higher and Standard Level. Four possibilities, and plenty of Town Square parents do not know which one is on the timetable.

Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic route: proof, functions, calculus, and at Higher Level proof by induction and contradiction, complex numbers and vectors. It rewards a student comfortable manipulating symbols and following an argument. Applications and Interpretation is the modelling route: statistics, regression, financial mathematics, and at Higher Level matrices and graph theory. It rewards a student who likes real data and uses technology confidently.

The pitfall is treating AI as the easy option. It is not easier, it is different. AI Standard Level students who chose it to avoid difficulty regularly meet hypothesis testing and regression with no statistical vocabulary and find it harder than the algebra they were avoiding. AI Higher Level contains matrices, graph theory and complex numbers, which genuinely surprises people who picked it expecting less abstraction.

The university question should be resolved first. Some mathematics, physics and engineering degrees specify Analysis and Approaches, and many specify Higher Level in a mathematics subject. Check the published entry requirements of the actual institutions under consideration, including UAE universities, for the year of entry rather than the current one. Reversing the choice after a term of Year 12 is painful where it is possible at all, and a tutor matched to the wrong route will teach correct mathematics the paper does not reward.

sections.heading: Where the marks actually go in IB maths
paragraphs: Students revise topics; examiners mark papers. Organising the work around the second is what separates a student who knows mathematics from one who scores it, and the loss patterns are consistent enough to plan against.

On the non-calculator paper, arithmetic slips and algebraic manipulation abandoned halfway. On the calculator paper, answers given with no stated method or model, so the reasoning marks are unavailable even when the number is right. On the Higher Level third paper, whole questions abandoned after one unfamiliar part when the later parts were accessible. And across every component, notation: a symbol used without definition, a line of working with no equals sign, an answer quoted to a precision the question never asked for.

The most expensive habit is stopping too early. Marks are available for method, and a student who computes several steps mentally and writes one line forfeits credit they genuinely earned. Changing that is a behaviour change rather than a knowledge gain, takes a few weeks of marked practice with a rule that every step goes on paper, and is probably the cheapest grade movement available in the subject.

The Exploration is the other large recoverable block, at 20% of the grade in every route. It is assessed on presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics — and difficulty is not on that list. A student who takes a topic they genuinely care about and handles it with mathematics appropriate to their course outscores one who attempts something ambitious, half understands it, and shows no sign of caring.
bullets: Non-calculator paper: arithmetic slips and manipulation left incomplete

sections.heading: The Exploration, and what coaching may legitimately do
paragraphs: A fifth of the maths grade comes from an independent piece of work, and most of what decides the mark happens in the fortnight when the topic is chosen rather than in the writing.

The criteria reward presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics. Personal engagement is where Town Square students lose most, and it cannot be added at the end — it has to be visible in the choice of question and in how the work is conducted. Reflection is the next biggest loss, written as a summary of steps taken rather than as genuine evaluation of what the mathematics showed and what its limits were.

What a tutor may do is substantial. Help find a topic with real engagement and workable mathematics. Check the mathematical level fits the course rather than the student's ambition. Explain what each criterion asks for and what it is worth. Read a draft the student has written and point out that notation is inconsistent, that the reflection is a summary, or that a step does not follow.

What a tutor may not do is produce the work: not write a section, not supply the calculations the student transcribes, not provide a model Exploration to adapt, not edit a draft to a finish so the submitted piece is substantially theirs. The student signs an authorship declaration and the supervisor signs alongside, and the IB withdraws awards for malpractice. This search result contains operators selling completed Internal Assessments — one advertises them at AED 3,750 — which risks the entire Diploma rather than one component. We also host no IB past papers, mark schemes or subject guides as downloads; they belong to the IB and we link the official source.

The scheduling argument has a price dimension worth making explicit. An in-home arrangement from Town Square costs more per hour and buys a worse hour, because the tutor's drive pushes the start past six. So the premium is paying for a journey that also degrades the product. For a young child who needs physical presence that trade can still be worth making. For a Diploma maths student it rarely is.

Monthly, Bestimate estimates AED 240-600 for one weekly hour at the budget band, AED 600-1,200 mid-tier and AED 1,000-2,000 or more for specialist exam-year work. Advertised packages include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599-1,799 for four in-home two-hour visits.

sections.heading: Ramadan, prayer times and the UAE school calendar
paragraphs: A maths plan written in September that ignores the UAE academic year will break by February, and maths breaks worse than other subjects because each session builds directly on the last. Continuity is the thing being bought.

Ramadan is the largest change. School days shorten, the evening reorganises around Iftar, and a student comfortable at six o'clock is not. Town Square families typically do one of three things: shift to a late-morning or early-afternoon slot, move to a post-Iftar slot, or pause part of the month and resume with a heavier block afterwards. All three work. Keeping the usual Tuesday at six does not. Content also sensibly shifts towards consolidation rather than new technique for that period.

Prayer times matter year-round and move through the calendar, so we set slots around them from the start rather than waiting for a family to raise it. The same applies to Islamic and public holidays, the long summer, and the travel weekends that are a normal part of life here — sessions continue while a family is away, because the tutor's location is already part of the arrangement rather than an obstacle to it.

The commitment we ask for is small: tell us the new pattern and we reset the fixed slot. What we work to avoid is the drift where a session is cancelled, then rescheduled, then cancelled, until nobody says out loud that the arrangement has ended. In maths that drift costs more than in any other subject, because the thread does not pick up where it was left.

sections.heading: What we will not promise about a maths grade
paragraphs: No grade guarantee. Not a specific number, not a points improvement, not a particular paper score. The variables that decide a maths grade — prior algebraic fluency, weeks remaining, whether the Exploration was started early, whether the student has ever been taught to show method — are not all under a tutor's control, and an offer that ignores that is a sales device rather than a commitment.

No statistics without a sample size, a date and a method, which means none published. No average score achieved by students we have taught, no percentage improved, no satisfaction figure, no self-generated star rating. Competitors publish such numbers routinely, sometimes in two conflicting versions on the same page, and almost never say how any of them was produced.

No regulator or awarding-body claim, and no examiner descriptions. IB Gram holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE, MoHRE, IB or Cambridge approval, accreditation, licence or partnership, has no office or centre anywhere in the UAE, and does not describe tutors as IB examiners because current examiner status is not something we can evidence. Examiner status also confers no access to marking, boundaries or paper content whatever is implied.

What we will give you is a verdict after the diagnostic: whether the gap is the algebraic foundation, paper technique or the Exploration, roughly how long each takes to move, and whether the time available is enough. Sometimes the answer is that it is not, and that concentrating on two of those rather than three is the better plan. We will also tell you when a proposed session time will not work for maths, rather than taking the booking.

faqs.question: What time can a maths session start after the Town Square school run?
faqs.answer: For a short run — South View in Remraam, or Fairgreen in The Sustainable City — around 4:15pm to 4:30pm. From GEMS Metropole in Motor City or Dubai Sports City in peak traffic, 4:45pm. From an inner-city school in Al Barsha or Silicon Oasis, closer to five, and many of those families choose an 8pm slot instead. These times exist only because nobody is driving to you; a visiting tutor leaving another part of Dubai in the same traffic realistically starts at half six.

faqs.question: Why does the hour matter more for maths than for other subjects?
faqs.answer: Because the work is cognitively dense in a particular way. A tired student can read a history chapter and retain something. A tired student cannot follow a derivation, cannot hold three variables in mind while rearranging an expression, and cannot sustain the twenty minutes of silent working a real past-paper question needs. Booking whichever slot is free is therefore a worse decision in maths than elsewhere, and it is the one families most often make because maths is the subject they worry about most.

faqs.question: Which weekly window suits a Year 13 maths student in Town Square?
faqs.answer: Usually 8pm to 9:30pm, and ninety minutes rather than sixty. Year 13 students work late anyway, are sharpest once the house is quiet, and need a block long enough to complete a past-paper section and mark it together rather than rushing the marking, which is the part that teaches. The 4:45pm window suits Year 12 and MYP students better, while attention is fresh enough for new technique. The 7pm slot looks convenient and consumes the student's own most productive independent hour.

faqs.question: How do I find out whether my child takes AA or AI?
faqs.answer: Ask the school, and ask for the level too — the full answer is one of four: Analysis and Approaches Higher or Standard, or Applications and Interpretation Higher or Standard. It is usually on the Year 11 subject choice form and on the Diploma timetable. It matters because the two courses have different syllabuses and different papers, so a tutor matched to the wrong one teaches correct mathematics in proportions the paper will not reward. We will not propose anybody before we know which of the four it is.

faqs.question: When in the Diploma is maths tutoring worth most?
faqs.answer: The first term of Year 12, by a wide margin. Everything in the course sits on algebraic fluency, so securing it early makes every later topic cheaper to teach. The Exploration topic should then be chosen in the second half of Year 12, while a good topic is still possible rather than merely an available one. By the spring of Year 13 the only remaining lever is paper technique, which is worth real marks but is smaller than foundations plus Exploration plus technique together.

faqs.question: Is Applications and Interpretation a lighter choice than Analysis and Approaches?
faqs.answer: No, and choosing it on that basis causes trouble. AI emphasises modelling, statistics, financial mathematics and the use of technology where AA emphasises algebra, proof and calculus. Students who pick AI to avoid difficulty frequently find hypothesis testing and regression harder than the algebra they were avoiding, because they arrive with no statistical vocabulary to think in. AI at Higher Level also contains matrices, graph theory and complex numbers. Choose on what the intended degree expects, verified from the institution's published requirement.

faqs.question: Does the Exploration really count for a fifth of the grade?
faqs.answer: Yes, in every IB maths course at both levels, and it is assessed on presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics. Difficulty is not on that list, which catches strong students out: an ambitious topic half understood with no visible engagement scores below a modest topic handled correctly by somebody who clearly cared. Because it is finished before exam revision begins, it is also the most recoverable block of marks in the course if addressed in Year 12 rather than Year 13.

faqs.question: How much Exploration help can a Town Square tutor legitimately give?
faqs.answer: A tutor can say that a step does not follow, that notation is inconsistent, or that a conclusion is not supported by the working — feedback on a draft the student has written is permitted and useful. What a tutor may not do is supply the calculations, write a section, provide a model Exploration to adapt, or edit the piece to a finish so it is substantially theirs. The student signs an authorship declaration and the supervisor signs alongside, and the IB withdraws awards for malpractice, so the line is practical.

faqs.question: Will a maths tutor come to our home in Town Square?
faqs.answer: Not one of ours. IB Gram delivers maths tuition to Town Square one-to-one over live video and makes no home visits anywhere in the UAE — in-home tutoring is a service we run in India only. Beyond that, the in-home model is particularly poor value for Diploma maths from this community: published rates are AED 180-500 an hour including travel, and the drive pushes the start past six, so you pay more per hour and buy a worse hour for the subject that tolerates it least.

faqs.question: What do Town Square families pay for IB maths help?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai figures read in October 2026: budget online AED 33-65 an hour (Tutopiya, EdFlik), qualified online subject tutors AED 150-300 with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200, IB specialists AED 200-450 and above with TutorChase at AED 270 and Bestimate giving AED 200-450 plus, in-home visits AED 180-500 including travel, and BartyED at AED 650 premium. Monthly, Bestimate estimates AED 240-600 budget, AED 600-1,200 mid and AED 1,000-2,000 plus for specialist exam-year work. Those belong to the providers named; we quote after the diagnostic.

faqs.question: How do maths sessions change during Ramadan here?
faqs.answer: They move, and planning the move beats improvising it. School days shorten and evenings reorganise around Iftar, so the usual slot stops working. Town Square families typically switch to a late-morning or early-afternoon session, move to post-Iftar, or pause part of the month and resume with a heavier block. Content also shifts sensibly towards consolidation rather than new technique for that period. Tell us the pattern and we reset the fixed slot, because in maths a run of cancellations costs more than in any other subject.

faqs.question: Is there an AA Higher Level specialist living near Town Square?
faqs.answer: Frequently not. The IB is around 7% of Dubai's 387,441 private-school pupils spread across the whole emirate, only the final two years sit the Diploma, and Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is one route of four. The pool who have taught it to final grade is small citywide, and most are serving school teachers whose permit code of conduct bars tutoring students enrolled at their own school. Town Square is also a newer community where residential build-out outran tutoring supply. Online matching removes distance from the problem.

faqs.question: What should we do in the six weeks before mocks?
faqs.answer: Technique, in order, and nothing else. First the rule that every step goes on paper, because method marks are being forfeited by mental arithmetic. Second, stating the model or method on calculator-paper answers, so reasoning marks become available. Third, past-paper sections in ninety-minute blocks, marked properly rather than discussed, with the error pattern deciding the next session. For Higher Level, dedicated work on the third paper, which most schools reach late. Content gaps larger than a topic or two are not realistically closable in six weeks.

faqs.question: Can one tutor take maths and physics for the same student?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and in this pairing there is a real argument for it: the algebraic and graphical demands overlap heavily, so one specialist can teach the rearrangement layer once rather than twice and stop a student treating the two subjects as unrelated. It also lets one person weigh a Physics investigation deadline against a maths mock instead of two tutors each optimising for their own subject. What we will not do is stretch a tutor across courses they do not genuinely teach to save a second match.

faqs.question: When are IB maths exams for Town Square students?
faqs.answer: UAE schools sit the May session. We publish no specific IB date, and the reason is worth stating: the IB's own site blocks automated checking, so no IB session or results date in this project has been confirmed from ibo.org, and we will not put an unverified date in front of a family who will plan around it. Get exact dates from your school's IB coordinator or ibo.org. For IGCSE siblings, Cambridge runs June and November series — February/March is India-only — and Pearson runs May/June and November.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-umm-al-sheif.tutorsIntro: Umm Al Sheif mathematics enquiries almost always name a component: Paper 1 without a calculator, Paper 3 at Higher Level, or an exploration that will not narrow down. We match from the named component to a tutor who teaches that paper repeatedly rather than to a general mathematics teacher.

intro.heading: Two courses, not one subject with two difficulties
paragraphs: The IB offers two mathematics courses at both Standard and Higher Level. Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic and proof-oriented route. Applications and Interpretation is the statistical and modelling route. They share five topic areas on paper, which makes them look like variations of the same thing, and they are not. The questions, the calculator rules and the university doors they open all differ.

The calculator rule is the cleanest illustration. In Analysis and Approaches, Paper 1 is sat without a graphical display calculator at both levels. In Applications and Interpretation, every paper allows one. A student who has spent two years with a calculator permanently available and then sits a non-calculator paper is in a different examination from the one they practised for, and the difference shows up in arithmetic slips rather than in understanding.

The second difference is Paper 3, which exists only at Higher Level in both courses. It is a sixty-minute paper carrying fifty-five marks across two extended problem-solving questions, where a student is led through an unfamiliar investigation in stages. It is a fifth of the Higher Level grade and it has no Standard Level equivalent, so it needs its own practice on its own past papers rather than more of Paper 2.

Third, the exploration. Both courses require an individual piece of mathematical writing marked out of twenty across five criteria: presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and use of mathematics. Six of those twenty marks go to personal engagement and reflection, which students treat as decoration around the mathematics. It is nearly a third of the Internal Assessment mark and it is written rather than calculated.

Umm Al Sheif is a villa district off Al Wasl Road between Umm Suqeim and Al Safa, with short school journeys and an unusually wide choice of session hours by Dubai standards. Most children are home between 14:45 and 15:45, so the limiting factor is the school's co-curricular programme rather than the road. That matters for mathematics specifically, because mathematics benefits more than most subjects from two shorter sessions a week than from one long one, and a household that can field two contacts a week will see accuracy work hold in a way a single weekly hour rarely achieves.

IB Gram delivers to Umm Al Sheif as one-to-one teaching over live video. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; in-home visits are a service we run only in India. What follows is the detail a parent needs to make a decision: the course choice and what it does to university options, how the five topics map to the papers, Paper 3, the calculator as an examinable skill, the exploration criterion by criterion, where marks go topic by topic, the transition into the Diploma, and what the local market charges.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-umm-al-sheif.programmesIntro: Mathematics runs through the whole IB continuum, and the handover points are where problems appear. Each stage below needs a different kind of mathematics teaching, and the transitions matter more than the content within any one stage.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme mathematics
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, with no external assessment, which suits conceptual understanding and can leave arithmetic fluency thin. A child who understands place value but cannot recall multiplication facts will struggle in Middle Years not because the ideas are hard but because every problem takes three times as long. Fluency work at this stage is cheap, quick and durable.
programmes.countryNote: Primary pupils from Umm Al Sheif mostly attend schools in Umm Suqeim, Al Safa or Jumeirah with journeys of ten to twenty minutes, so they are often home before 15:15. Two fifteen-minute fluency sessions a week fit easily into that and are more effective at this age than a single hour, which is longer than most nine-year-olds can sustain on arithmetic.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme mathematics
programmes.description: Marked against four criteria: knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Each runs one to eight. Investigating patterns is where strong arithmetic students lose marks, because it asks for generalisation and justification rather than a correct answer. Teaching a student to write a general rule and justify it is the main job here.
programmes.countryNote: Several Umm Suqeim and Al Safa schools run the full continuum, so many Umm Al Sheif students move from Middle Years straight into the Diploma in the same building. The hidden risk is timed practice: a student who scored sixes on criteria-based tasks may never have sat a timed mathematics paper, which the Diploma demands from the first term.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme mathematics
programmes.description: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, at Standard or Higher Level. Standard Level is prescribed at 150 teaching hours and Higher Level at 240, which is the clearest statement of the difference in volume. Papers 1 and 2 carry forty per cent each at Standard Level; at Higher Level that becomes thirty, thirty and twenty with Paper 3, plus twenty for the exploration.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma students in the Umm Suqeim, Al Safa and Al Sufouh schools often have study periods after a 15:30 finish, so 17:00 and 19:30 are both workable here. For Higher Level mathematics specifically, two sessions a week through the first year is a better investment than three a week in the spring of the second, because Paper 3 technique takes months rather than weeks.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme with a DP mathematics course
programmes.description: Where a school offers the Career-related Programme, a mathematics course taken inside it is examined on exactly the same papers with the same weightings and the same exploration. The qualification differs; the mathematics assessment does not. A student on this route needs identical teaching to a full Diploma candidate in that course and should be matched the same way.
programmes.countryNote: Very few schools in the Jumeirah and Umm Suqeim cluster run the Career-related Programme, so most Umm Al Sheif families are comparing Diploma mathematics against A Level Mathematics instead. If your child is on it, say so at matching, because the component weightings a tutor plans around are the Diploma ones.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-umm-al-sheif.subjectsIntro: Mathematics is one subject on a timetable and several distinct skill sets in an examination. These are the areas Umm Al Sheif families ask about, with what each actually demands.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches SL
subjects.description: Paper 1 without a calculator and Paper 2 with one, forty per cent each, plus the exploration at twenty. Algebraic manipulation under time pressure is the deciding skill, and most lost marks on Paper 1 are arithmetic or sign errors in work the student understood perfectly.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL
subjects.description: Thirty, thirty and twenty across three papers with the exploration at twenty. Proof, complex numbers and the depth of the calculus section are the hard content, and Paper 3 is the format shock. Students need proof-writing practice specifically, since it is marked on structure not just conclusion.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation SL
subjects.description: Both papers permit a calculator, so calculator fluency is examinable rather than convenient. Statistical tests, regression and modelling carry the content, and marks are lost by producing a correct output without stating what it means in context.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation HL
subjects.description: Adds matrices, graph theory, differential equations and heavier statistics, with Paper 3 as an extended modelling investigation. The calculator demands are substantial and specific, and a student who has not drilled the menus loses time rather than understanding.

subjects.name: The mathematical exploration
subjects.description: Twenty marks across presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and use of mathematics, with twelve to twenty pages recommended. The decisive move is narrowing the topic; a student with a question too broad to finish loses marks in four of the five criteria at once.

subjects.name: Paper 3, Higher Level only
subjects.description: Sixty minutes, fifty-five marks, two extended problem-solving questions that lead a student through unfamiliar territory in stages. It rewards reading each part carefully, using the previous part's result, and showing reasoning. It cannot be prepared for by doing more Paper 2 questions.

subjects.name: Graphical display calculator technique
subjects.description: Solving numerically, finding intersections, regression with its coefficient, normal and binomial distributions, numerical derivatives and definite integrals. These are examined skills with their own error modes, and fluency is built by drilling the menus rather than by understanding the mathematics better.

subjects.name: Proof and reasoning
subjects.levels: Analysis and Approaches, HL in particular
subjects.description: Direct proof, proof by contradiction, induction and counterexample. Marked on the validity of each step, so a student who reaches the right conclusion by an unjustified route scores poorly. Three or four sessions on proof structure typically pay for themselves at Higher Level.

subjects.name: Statistics and probability
subjects.description: Distributions, hypothesis testing, correlation and regression. The recurring loss is interpretation: a student calculates a coefficient correctly and then says it shows causation, or quotes a probability without stating the condition it was calculated under.

subjects.name: Calculus
subjects.levels: Both courses, substantially deeper in AA HL
subjects.description: Differentiation, integration, kinematics and, at Higher Level in Analysis, techniques including substitution and parts. Chain-rule errors inside composite functions and sign errors in definite integrals account for a large share of the lost marks at this level.

sections.heading: Analysis or Applications: the choice that follows your child to university
paragraphs: This is the most consequential decision in Diploma mathematics and it is frequently made on the basis of which course a student finds easier in Year 11. Analysis and Approaches is algebraic and proof-oriented, with a non-calculator Paper 1 at both levels. Applications and Interpretation is statistical and modelling-led, with a calculator permitted on every paper. Both are respectable courses; they are not interchangeable at the point of applying to university.

The pattern across competitive admissions is that mathematics-intensive degrees, engineering, physics, mathematics itself and many economics courses, commonly expect Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. Courses in the life sciences, business, psychology and much of the social sciences accept either, and some explicitly accept Applications at Higher Level. The only safe method is to read the stated entry requirement on each university's own admissions page, because they differ and they change.

For families planning on a UAE institution, the same instruction applies with more force. Universities in the Emirates publish their own International Baccalaureate entry requirements, and engineering routes in particular tend to specify the analytical course. No Ministry of Education equivalency figure for IB points has been read on an official source, so this page publishes none; anyone quoting one without a Ministry citation is guessing on your behalf.

The practical advice is to settle the question in Year 11 rather than in the first term of the Diploma. Two sessions on current attainment against the Analysis specification will tell you whether that course is realistic, and a move after the first term is disruptive and sometimes impossible. A tutor cannot make the decision, but a tutor can tell you what the evidence says.

sections.heading: The five topics and how they land in the papers
paragraphs: Both mathematics courses are organised into the same five topic areas: number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, and calculus. That shared structure is why the two courses look similar in a prospectus. What differs is the depth and emphasis inside each area, and how the resulting questions are distributed across the papers.

The prescribed teaching time states the difference bluntly. Standard Level is 150 hours and Higher Level is 240. That extra ninety hours is not revision of the same material; it is additional content, and it is concentrated in calculus and in the course-specific areas. A student moving from Standard to Higher Level mid-course is not working harder at the same syllabus; they are taking on roughly a third more of it.

Paper distribution matters for revision planning. At Standard Level the two papers carry forty per cent each, so an even split of practice is reasonable. At Higher Level the split becomes thirty, thirty and twenty, which means Paper 3 deserves a fifth of the practice time and almost never gets it. Students report revising Paper 1 and Paper 2 and then meeting Paper 3 as a format they have seen twice.

The table below maps the topics to where they bite. Use it to audit a revision schedule rather than to build one from scratch: if a topic area has had no attention in six weeks and appears on both papers, that is the gap to close first.

sections.heading: Paper 3 at Higher Level: what a scaffolded investigation asks for
paragraphs: Paper 3 runs for sixty minutes and carries fifty-five marks across two extended problem-solving questions. A student is led through an unfamiliar situation in parts, where each part builds on the last. It exists only at Higher Level and it is worth twenty per cent of the grade. Nothing in the Standard Level course prepares anybody for its shape.

The skills it rewards are specific and teachable. Read the whole question before starting any part, because part (a) usually exists to generate a result part (d) needs. Carry results forward exactly rather than rounding and reusing. Show reasoning, since marks are allocated to visible steps and a correct final answer with no working scores a fraction of what it could. Write a sentence in words when a part asks for an interpretation.

The most common failure is abandonment. A student stalls on part (b), spends twenty minutes there, and never reaches parts (c) to (f) where marks were available independently of (b). Teaching a student to park a part, state an assumption, and continue is worth more on this paper than additional content. It is a discipline rather than a skill, and it takes four or five timed attempts to establish.

Preparation is therefore format practice on genuine Paper 3 questions under timed conditions, with the mark scheme read afterwards line by line. Doing more Paper 2 questions does not prepare a student for Paper 3, and it is the single most common misallocation of revision time at Higher Level in both mathematics courses.

sections.heading: The graphical display calculator is an examined skill
paragraphs: Parents often assume a calculator is a convenience. In these courses it is examinable equipment with its own error modes, and that is most true in Applications and Interpretation, where every paper permits it. A student who understands regression perfectly and cannot produce the coefficient on their own machine inside ninety seconds is losing marks to menus rather than to mathematics.

The skills are finite and can be drilled in a handful of sessions: solving an equation numerically, finding the intersection of two graphs, running a regression and reading its coefficient, calculating normal and binomial probabilities and their inverses, producing a numerical derivative and a definite integral, and generating a sequence in a table. That is most of what the papers require, and most students have never been taught them systematically.

There is a second, quieter problem. Schools teach to whichever model the department has standardised, and students who buy a different model follow video tutorials for a machine they do not own. The menus differ, and under examination pressure that difference costs real time. Settle on the school's model, learn that one, and make sure the tutor can work with it.

For Analysis and Approaches the mirror-image risk applies. Paper 1 is sat without a calculator at both levels, so two years of permanent calculator access produces arithmetic that is competent only with support. Non-calculator practice has to be deliberate and regular from the first term, not introduced in the spring when it reveals itself as a problem.

sections.heading: The exploration, criterion by criterion
paragraphs: The exploration is twenty per cent of the mathematics grade, marked out of twenty, and the marks are published: presentation four, mathematical communication four, personal engagement three, reflection three, and use of mathematics six. Twelve to twenty pages is the recommended length. Those numbers should be in front of a student from the first day of the project, and in practice they usually are not.

Four of the five criteria are decided by the choice of topic. A question too broad to finish produces thin mathematics, disorganised presentation, shallow reflection and a struggle with communication, all at once. Narrowing is therefore the highest-value work a tutor does here, and it is also the work students resist, because a narrow question feels less impressive than a grand one.

Personal engagement and reflection together carry six of the twenty marks and are earned by writing about process: why this topic, which approach was tried and abandoned, what the result actually means, what the limitations are. Students treat this as filler around the mathematics. It is nearly a third of the mark and it is the part a tutor can help with most safely, because it is entirely the student's own thinking being made explicit.

The boundary matters here more than anywhere. A tutor may explain the criteria, question the topic, challenge the mathematics chosen, and say why a section is weak. No tutor at IB Gram will write the exploration, draft it or edit it to completion. The school supervisor signs the work off and should know that outside support exists; a tutor who suggests otherwise is creating a risk that falls on your child.

sections.heading: From Middle Years or IGCSE into Diploma mathematics
paragraphs: The transition into Diploma mathematics defeats more Umm Al Sheif students than the Diploma content does. A student arriving from the Middle Years Programme has been assessed against four criteria on extended tasks, often with access to resources and time. A student arriving from IGCSE has sat timed written papers but on a narrower syllabus with far more structured questions.

Each route has a characteristic gap. Middle Years students frequently arrive without timed paper experience, so the first Diploma assessment is their first encounter with pacing and with the requirement to produce correct work quickly. IGCSE students arrive with timed experience but meet unstructured questions for the first time, where nothing tells them which method to use.

The algebraic step is real in both cases. Diploma mathematics assumes fluent manipulation of expressions that IGCSE treats as the hardest material on the paper. A student who was comfortable at IGCSE because the algebra appeared in predictable forms will find the Diploma version unrecognisable, and the fix is a few weeks of concentrated manipulation practice rather than a conceptual intervention.

The best window is the summer between the two, or the spring before it. Three or four sessions on the specific gap, timed practice for continuum students and unstructured problem work for IGCSE students, makes the first Diploma term materially easier. It is also the cheapest mathematics tutoring a family will ever buy, because it is not competing with deadlines, with mock revision or with an exploration draft for the student's remaining hours. Nobody is panicking, which means the work can be slow and thorough.

sections.heading: Umm Al Sheif practicalities, and what mathematics tutoring costs here
paragraphs: Mathematics is the subject where session frequency matters most, and Umm Al Sheif is well placed for it. Journeys to the Umm Suqeim, Al Safa and Al Sufouh schools are short, most children are home between 14:45 and 15:45, and the limiting factor is the co-curricular programme rather than traffic. Two shorter sessions a week are genuinely schedulable here, which is harder in the outer communities.

On price, the Dubai market is public if you look for it and this page states it with sources rather than hiding behind a consultation. University-student tutors online advertise from around AED 33 to 52 at Tutopiya and AED 45 to 65 at EdFlik on their own pages. A qualified subject tutor online sits at roughly AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, and TutorChase quoting around AED 270.

Above that, specialists run AED 200 to 450 and beyond, and premium named tutors are quoted as high as AED 650 at BartyED. In-home visits in Dubai are quoted at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel priced into the figure, which is a real part of why in-home costs more. None of these figures is an IB Gram rate card; they are the market, published so you can judge any quote, ours included.

For mathematics the sensible allocation is frequency at the middle band rather than scarcity at the top. Two sessions a week with a qualified subject tutor through the first Diploma year will usually do more than a handful of premium hours in the spring of the second, because Paper 3 technique and non-calculator arithmetic are built by repetition. The exception is a single narrow component review, where the top band can be worth it.

process.title: Name the course, not just maths
process.description: Tell us Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, and Standard or Higher Level. Those four combinations are four different jobs. If you are not sure, the front of a past paper or the subject title on a report will say, and a two-minute email to the school will confirm it.

process.title: Send the marked paper and the error pattern
process.description: A mock script or a marked class test tells us whether the losses are algebraic slips, calculator fluency, interpretation or pacing. Those four have different remedies and different timescales, and guessing between them is how families end up buying hours that do not move anything.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: One per family, before payment and with no card details taken. Ask the tutor what Paper 1 is worth at your child's level and whether a calculator is permitted on it. A specialist answers instantly. Afterwards, check whether your child can now do a question type they could not do an hour earlier.

process.title: Set frequency before duration
process.description: For mathematics, two shorter sessions a week usually beat one long one, because the gap between contacts is where accuracy work either consolidates or decays. Decide the rhythm first, then the length, then agree what the next eight weeks should measurably achieve.

process.title: Keep an error log and review it
process.description: Every session ends with the errors recorded, not just corrected. At eight weeks the log shows whether sign errors, chain-rule slips or angle-mode mistakes have actually stopped recurring. If they have not, we change the tutor or the approach rather than adding hours.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the exact mathematics course
whyPoints.description: Analysis Higher Level and Applications Standard Level are different jobs needing different teachers. We match on course and level together, which is why those are the first two things we ask for, and it is why a specialist is usually available even for narrow combinations.

whyPoints.title: Paper structure stated, not implied
whyPoints.description: Paper 1 in Analysis is non-calculator at both levels. Paper 3 is sixty minutes and fifty-five marks at Higher Level only. The exploration is twenty marks across five named criteria. These are published facts, and a provider unwilling to state them is hoping you will not ask.

whyPoints.title: Frequency over length for mathematics
whyPoints.description: Accuracy and fluency are built by repetition, so two shorter weekly sessions usually outperform one long one. Umm Al Sheif's short school journeys make that schedulable here in a way it is not in communities an hour from school.

whyPoints.title: The calculator treated as examinable
whyPoints.description: Menus, regression coefficients, inverse normal and angle mode are drilled deliberately, because under time pressure those cost marks that have nothing to do with understanding. We also work to your school's standardised model rather than a different one.

whyPoints.title: Rates from the market with sources
whyPoints.description: Every dirham figure here belongs to a named provider or a published rate table with its date, and none is presented as our price. You can hold any quote against the band it sits in, which is more than most pages in this market will allow you to do.

whyPoints.title: The exploration boundary in writing
whyPoints.description: A tutor narrows the topic, challenges the mathematics and explains the criteria. Nobody at IB Gram writes, drafts or edits an exploration, and the school supervisor should know support exists. In a market where completed Internal Assessments are sold, that line is worth stating plainly.

faqs.question: Should we look for an IB maths tutor in Umm Al Sheif who teaches Analysis or Applications?
faqs.answer: Whichever course your child is actually taking, and the two are not interchangeable. Analysis and Approaches is algebraic and proof-oriented with a non-calculator Paper 1 at both levels. Applications and Interpretation is statistical and modelling-led with a calculator on every paper. A tutor strong in one is not automatically useful in the other, because the error modes differ: algebraic slips against failures of interpretation. Check the subject title on a report card or the front of a past paper before you book anybody.

faqs.question: Does an Umm Al Sheif Analysis student really sit Paper 1 with no calculator?
faqs.answer: In Analysis and Approaches, yes, at both Standard and Higher Level. In Applications and Interpretation a graphical display calculator is permitted on every paper. This single difference catches out more students than any content gap, because two years of permanent calculator access produces arithmetic that is competent only with support. If your child takes Analysis, deliberate non-calculator practice should be running from the first term rather than discovered as a problem in the spring.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a maths tutor to a villa in Umm Al Sheif?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Mathematics lessons for Umm Al Sheif families are one to one over live video, with a shared whiteboard where every line of working is visible and saved afterwards. For mathematics specifically that whiteboard record is an advantage, because a worked solution can be reread before the next paper instead of being lost in a notebook.

faqs.question: How much of the Higher Level maths grade is Paper 3?
faqs.answer: Twenty per cent, from a sixty-minute paper carrying fifty-five marks across two extended problem-solving questions. It exists only at Higher Level in both mathematics courses. Papers 1 and 2 carry thirty per cent each and the exploration the remaining twenty. The practical consequence is that Paper 3 deserves a fifth of the revision time, and students almost never give it that, because it is unlike anything they have practised and is therefore easy to defer.

faqs.question: How do we stop my son running out of time on Paper 3?
faqs.answer: Teach him to park a part rather than fight it. The characteristic Paper 3 failure is spending twenty minutes on part (b) and never reaching parts (d) to (f), where marks were available independently. The discipline is to state an assumption, move on, and return if time allows. It takes four or five timed attempts on genuine Paper 3 questions to establish, and it is worth far more than additional content work at Higher Level.

faqs.question: What is the maths exploration marked out of, and where do marks go?
faqs.answer: Twenty marks across five criteria: presentation four, mathematical communication four, personal engagement three, reflection three, and use of mathematics six. Twelve to twenty pages is the recommended length. Students lose most in personal engagement and reflection, which together carry six marks and are earned by writing about choices made, approaches abandoned and what the result means. Treating that writing as padding around the mathematics costs nearly a third of the Internal Assessment mark.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help choose an exploration topic without crossing the line?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the single most valuable thing a tutor does on this component. A topic too broad to finish damages four of the five criteria simultaneously, so narrowing it is where the marks are won. A tutor may question the topic, challenge the mathematics chosen, explain each criterion and say why a section is weak. Nobody at IB Gram writes, drafts or edits an exploration. The school supervisor signs the work off and should know that support exists.

faqs.question: Which calculator skills are actually examined in IB mathematics?
faqs.answer: Solving equations numerically, finding graph intersections, running a regression and reading its coefficient, normal and inverse normal calculations, binomial probabilities, numerical derivatives and definite integrals, and generating sequences in a table. Angle mode belongs on the list too, because degrees against radians invalidates every answer in a trigonometry question. These are finite, drillable skills, and most students have never been taught them systematically on the model their school has standardised.

faqs.question: My daughter understands the maths but loses marks anyway, so why?
faqs.answer: Almost always one of four things, and the marked script tells you which. Sign errors and dropped terms in multi-step rearrangement. Chain-rule mistakes inside composite functions. A correct statistical calculation followed by a causal claim the data cannot support. Or pacing, where the last question is routinely unattempted. Each has a different remedy and a different timescale, and the common mistake is to treat all four as a need for more content teaching when none of them is.

faqs.question: How hard is the jump from MYP maths into the Diploma course?
faqs.answer: The content step is manageable; the assessment step is not, and it catches continuum students in particular. Middle Years mathematics is marked against four criteria on extended tasks, often with resources and time available. Diploma mathematics is examined on timed papers where correct work has to be produced quickly. Many Umm Al Sheif students arrive in the Diploma having never sat a timed mathematics paper. Three to five weeks of timed section practice in the preceding summer removes most of that shock.

faqs.question: Is the IGCSE to Diploma maths gap different from the MYP one?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in the opposite direction. IGCSE students arrive with timed paper experience and solid procedures, but meet unstructured questions for the first time, where nothing in the wording tells them which method to use. The algebraic step is also real: Diploma mathematics assumes fluent manipulation of expressions that IGCSE treats as its hardest material. Four to six weeks of open problem work, rather than more procedural practice, is what closes that particular gap.

faqs.question: Will Applications and Interpretation close an engineering route for my child?
faqs.answer: Several publish entry requirements that specify the analytical course for engineering routes, but requirements differ between institutions and change between cycles, so the only reliable method is to read the stated requirement on each university's own admissions page. No Ministry of Education equivalency threshold for IB points has been read on an official source, so this page does not publish one. Treat any provider quoting an IB points figure for equivalency without a Ministry citation with real caution.

faqs.question: Is twice a week really better than one longer maths session?
faqs.answer: For most students, yes, and mathematics is the subject where it matters most. Accuracy and fluency are built by repetition, and the gap between sessions is where consolidation either happens or decays. Two forty-five or sixty-minute contacts halve that gap. The exception is a student whose problem is conceptual rather than procedural, where a single longer session gives room to build an idea properly. The marked script usually makes clear which case you are in.

faqs.question: What does maths tutoring cost in Dubai at the moment?
faqs.answer: Taking published market figures rather than our own, university-student tutors online advertise from around AED 33 to 65 an hour, a qualified subject tutor online runs roughly AED 150 to 300, specialists sit at AED 200 to 450 and above, and premium named tutors have been quoted as high as AED 650. One weekly hour at the middle band works out at roughly AED 600 to 1,200 a month on Bestimate's estimate. For mathematics, frequency at the middle band usually beats scarcity at the top.

faqs.question: What if no Higher Level maths specialist is free at our hour?
faqs.answer: We say so instead of substituting a generalist. Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level in a fixed evening slot is one of the tighter combinations in this market, and occasionally nobody suitable is available. Common Standard Level requests are usually matched within a few days. Being told honestly leaves you time to look elsewhere, which is far more useful than discovering in session three that the tutor has never taught Paper 3 and is reading the question for the first time alongside your child.

From those we can see whether the losses are algebraic, calculator-driven, interpretive or about pacing, and which of those the remaining weeks can realistically fix. Then your child meets a specialist in that exact course on a free trial lesson before anything is paid. Lessons run live online, one to one, twice a week if that suits the Umm Al Sheif timetable better.

intro.heading: Why the maths slot is the hardest hour to place in an Umm Suqeim week
paragraphs: Umm Suqeim is a strip of villa communities between Jumeirah Beach Road and Al Wasl Road, numbered one to three as you move inland and west. Almost nobody here walks to school. Children leave for Kings' School Dubai, Raffles World Academy, Jumeirah College, Jumeirah English Speaking School, Horizon English School or across to Dubai College and Dubai American Academy, and the return leg lands somewhere between a quarter past three and twenty past four depending on which gate and which bus. That spread of an hour is the whole problem with booking a maths lesson in this neighbourhood, and it is why so many weekly slots quietly collapse by half-term.

Mathematics is the subject least forgiving of a collapsed slot. A Diploma student who misses two weeks of English can read the text at the weekend and catch up. A student who misses two weeks of Analysis and Approaches Higher Level during the calculus sequence has lost the scaffolding that the next four topics stand on, and the gap shows up months later as an inability to start a Paper 2 question rather than an inability to finish one. Maths is cumulative in a way that no amount of revision at the end repairs cheaply.

So the sensible order is backwards. Fix the hour first, then choose the tutor who can teach at that hour, then plan the content. That inversion is the single most useful thing on this page. Families who pick a tutor first and then try to fit the diary around them end up moving the lesson three times, dropping to fortnightly, and concluding that tutoring does not work for their child. Families who fix a protected slot on a fixed day keep it for two years.

Online delivery is what makes a fixed slot possible here. IB Gram teaches UAE students one-to-one over live video and does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. That is a limit, and it is stated plainly rather than buried. What it buys an Umm Suqeim family is real: the lesson starts at the minute it is booked whether or not Beach Road is moving, the tutor is chosen for the exact route and level your child sits rather than for living within a twenty-minute drive, and a 7.30pm start on a Tuesday is an ordinary request instead of an expensive one.

The rest of this page is written in that order. First the week, then the route choice between Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, then the papers and where marks actually leak, then the Exploration with its criteria named letter by letter, then what the Dubai market charges with the sources attached, then how to start and what happens when the specialist you want is full.
