sections.heading: Paired and group French: where sharing works and where it does not
paragraphs: Sharing a session is the most common way Dubai families try to reduce the bill, and it works for some of the subject and not for other parts of it. The economics are straightforward: two students at a reduced rate each costs less per family than two separate hours. The teaching question is what gets halved, and in a language subject one of the four criteria gets halved much more severely than the others.

Reading, listening and written feedback share well. A reading passage can be set at a level both students can access, listening tasks are answered individually and discussed together, and written work is marked separately so neither student loses anything at all on Criterion D. For those three criteria a shared session is close to a free saving, provided the two students are genuinely within a phase of each other.

Speaking does not share. Criterion C improves on time spent talking, and a shared hour halves it. Worse, in a pair one student usually dominates and the quieter one practises less than half, so the arithmetic is more punishing than it looks. For a student whose target is speaking, two short individual slots a week at the same monthly cost is a better purchase than a shared hour at a lower rate.

There is one hard limit worth stating. Where two students are two or more phases apart, we decline the pair rather than run it, because the session is then pitched wrongly for at least one of them and both families are paying for something that only half works. A sibling discount is not worth a term of teaching the younger child above their level and the older one below theirs.

sections.heading: The francophone demand curve in Dubai, and what it does to prices
paragraphs: French pricing in Dubai behaves differently from most subjects because supply and demand are unevenly matched across the phases. The city holds a substantial francophone professional population and two French-system schools, which means a large supply of fluent speakers available at the budget and mid bands. That keeps beginner and middle-phase French cheaper here than it would be in a city without that population.

At the top of the subject the picture reverses. The teachers who can work on Phase 5 and 6 register, analytical vocabulary and unadapted text are mostly employed by schools, and the private pool is small. So the cost curve across the phases is unusually flat at the bottom and unusually steep at the top, which is the opposite of what parents expect when they assume prices rise smoothly with age.

Demand is seasonal on top of that, and the seasons are set by school calendars rather than by public exams. Requests concentrate in the weeks before internal assessment and reporting windows, and in the run-up to Diploma option choices at the end of MYP 4 and MYP 5. The specialist end books out first in each of those periods, so families arriving late choose from whatever remains rather than from the whole market.

The practical consequence is a timing decision worth more than a negotiation. Starting a block mid-term, when diaries are open, buys a better teacher at a calmer price than starting three weeks before a report. KHDA's confirmation in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for 2026-27 is a useful reminder that the tutoring line is the part of the education budget nobody caps, which makes the timing discipline yours to impose.

sections.heading: Budgeting French across MYP 4 and MYP 5
paragraphs: These are the two years where French spending actually changes an outcome, because the MYP 5 record determines the Diploma route and the route determines two further years of cost. Treating them as a single two-year budget rather than as a term-by-term decision tends to produce both a lower total and a better result, since the work can be placed where it has leverage instead of where the panic happens to be.

A sensible shape for a student aiming to protect French B Higher Level looks like this. A targeted block in MYP 4 on whichever of reading or writing is weaker, since those are the criteria a school examines when allocating Higher Level. A lighter term afterwards, or none at all, with school provision carrying the load. Then a short text-type block in the first half of MYP 5, timed to the school's internal portfolio deadlines rather than to any public window.

At mid-band market rates that comes to roughly a term of weekly sessions plus two short blocks, rather than two continuous years of weekly hours. The saving against an open-ended arrangement across the same period is considerable, and the result is usually better because each block has a target and an end. The money goes where the criterion is rather than where the calendar is.

One final note on the ePortfolio year. MYP 5 Language Acquisition is assessed through a moderated portfolio of the student's own work rather than an on-screen examination, so there is no single date to buy revision for. What is worth paying for is text-type range and the student's own command of the descriptors, since a portfolio that repeats one register caps itself. A tutor may teach and give feedback on the student's work and must not produce any part of it.

sections.heading: Hidden extras: marking, materials, cancellations and tax
paragraphs: Four things routinely appear after a rate has been agreed, and all four are avoidable by asking in advance. Marking is the largest. An hour of teaching and an hour that includes setting, banding and returning a written task are different products, and when marking is charged separately the headline rate stops being comparable. Ask whether it is inside the figure and what the turnaround is, then compare quotes on that basis rather than on the hourly number alone.

Materials are the second. For MYP French the honest position is that most of what is needed is the student's own school tasks plus authentic text, so there should be little to buy. Treat a required course pack with some suspicion, and note that official syllabus documents, past papers and mark schemes belong to the awarding bodies and should be referenced and linked rather than copied or supplied as downloads by anybody.

Cancellation terms are the third and the most commonly disputed. Dubai evenings produce genuine clashes, so the question is how much notice avoids a charge and whether a missed session can be deferred inside a block. Get the answer before booking rather than during the first argument about it, and prefer a block with a deferral rule over a standing slot that is simply lost when a fixture is rescheduled.

Tax is the fourth, and the only honest thing to say is narrow. We will tell you whether a figure we quote is inclusive of any applicable tax; we will not characterise the UAE VAT treatment of tuition generally, because that requires a Federal Tax Authority source and is not something to take from a tutoring page. Ask any provider to state plainly whether their quoted AED figure is what will leave your account.

sections.heading: Three ways Dubai families overpay for French
paragraphs: The first is paying for discovery. A tutor who spends four sessions working out what is wrong is being paid at a teaching rate to do a diagnosis, and the diagnosis is a forty-minute job if somebody asks the right questions. Send a page of written French and the last report before the first session, insist that the first session ends with a phase estimate and a named target, and the four weeks that would have gone on orientation go on teaching instead.

The second is paying for the wrong criterion. Most Dubai French students have an uneven profile, and more conversation practice for a student whose speaking is already their strongest criterion adds very little to a grade however enjoyable the sessions are. Half the marks in the subject sit in reading and writing. Buying against the criterion that is actually losing marks is the single largest saving available, and it costs nothing to work out first.

The third is the arrangement that never ends. An open-ended weekly hour with warm feedback and no measurement will run for as long as a family keeps paying, because stopping feels like giving up on the child rather than on the arrangement. Blocks with named targets and end dates cost more per hour and far less in total. A provider who resists being measured that way has told you something useful about the next two years.

None of the three is about hourly rates, which is why negotiating one is usually the least productive conversation available. Decide the criterion, decide the pattern, agree what marking is included, fix an end date, and the total falls by more than any discount would have delivered. Then judge the spending on a banded script rather than on how the sessions felt.

process.description: Those two things let the first session start on diagnosis instead of orientation, which is the cheapest saving in this whole process. Include the phase and the criterion bands if the school prints them, and say which pattern you are considering, weekly or twice-weekly.

process.title: Free first session, then one figure
process.description: Sixty minutes ending with a phase estimate, a named target criterion and a band on marked work. Our quote comes after that, as a single hourly figure with setting and marking inside it, and we say which session pattern we would recommend and why. No card is taken for the trial.

process.title: Agree the pattern, the end date and the terms
process.description: Weekly hour, two short slots, or a fixed-price block. We state the cancellation rule, the deferral rule inside a block, and whether the quoted figure is inclusive of any applicable tax. The rate holds for the term and is not re-quoted because a reporting window is coming.

process.title: Review at the end of the block, not by default
process.description: A block ends and gets a decision rather than rolling over. A fresh task banded against the same descriptor set shows whether the money moved anything. Buy another block, change the target, change the tutor, or stop; all four are real answers and we will say which we would pick.

whyPoints.title: One figure, marking included
whyPoints.description: The quote covers teaching, setting and banding written work, with the turnaround stated. Rates that exclude marking look cheaper and cost more per band moved, which is the most common way a French tutoring bill grows after the price has been agreed.

whyPoints.title: The travel line, shown rather than buried
whyPoints.description: Published in-home rates in Dubai imply AED 50 to 150 an hour of journey against online bands. We do not sell home visits in the UAE, and rather than argue about formats we publish the arithmetic so a family can judge what that component buys.

whyPoints.title: Patterns compared at equal spend
whyPoints.description: A weekly hour, two short slots and a fortnightly long session cost similar amounts and produce very different results in a language subject. We recommend by criterion rather than by convenience, including when that means selling fewer hours this term.

whyPoints.title: Blocks that end
whyPoints.description: Every block carries a named target and a stated end date agreed before it starts. Open-ended weekly arrangements are the most expensive thing in this market, not because the rate is high but because nothing ever triggers the decision to stop.

whyPoints.description: Phase 5 and 6 French is thin across the whole Dubai market, including with us. Where nobody suitable is free for your slot we say so and name the honest alternative at the rate that matches what that person actually does.

faqs.question: How much does an MYP French home tutor cost in Dubai?
faqs.answer: In-home one-to-one across Dubai is published at AED 180 to 350 an hour in Bestimate's 2026 rate table, with independent listings reaching AED 500 and monthly packages of AED 1,599 to 1,799 advertised for four two-hour visits. Travel sits inside those figures. Online one-to-one with a qualified subject teacher runs roughly AED 150 to 300, and programme specialists AED 200 to 450 and above. IB Gram does not sell home visits in the UAE, so those in-home figures are market context rather than an offer from us.

faqs.question: What does the travel part of an in-home French rate actually cost?
faqs.answer: Comparing the published ranges gives a usable estimate. Against an online qualified-teacher band of about AED 150 to 300 an hour, in-home rates of AED 180 to 500 imply somewhere between AED 50 and 150 an hour of journey, varying with distance and the time of day. A family in Mudon or Remraam sits near the top of that; one near the Trade Centre sits near the bottom. It is an honest cost honestly charged, and it buys no teaching whatsoever.

faqs.question: Is paying extra for a native French speaker worth it in the MYP?
faqs.answer: For speaking and listening, often yes; for written work, frequently not. Dubai has a large francophone population, so native speakers are plentiful at the budget and mid bands and are good value for oral-only slots where an authentic model matters. What is scarce is somebody who can band a piece of writing against phase descriptors and name the next move. Test it directly: send a script and ask for a band and a next step. Specificity in the answer is worth more than fluency in the speaker.

faqs.question: Is a ninety-minute French session better value than an hour?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and in-home economics rather than teaching is what produces the longer session. Concentration on grammar correction and oral practice is not linear, so the back half of a long session tends to deliver less than the front half. A ninety-minute minimum also raises the monthly bill by half at an identical hourly rate. For most MYP students a weekly hour with a marked task, or two shorter slots, buys more movement at the same or lower monthly spend.

faqs.question: How much should we budget for French across MYP 4 and MYP 5?
faqs.answer: Think in blocks rather than in continuous terms. A sensible shape is a targeted block in MYP 4 on whichever of reading or writing is weaker, a lighter term or none afterwards with school provision carrying the load, then a short text-type block in the first half of MYP 5 timed to the school's internal portfolio deadlines. At mid-band market rates that is roughly a term of weekly sessions plus two short blocks, which costs materially less than two years of weekly hours and usually works better.

faqs.question: Does sharing a French session with a classmate cut the cost?
faqs.answer: It reduces the per-family figure and only works for part of the subject. Reading, listening and written feedback share well, because the material can be pitched for both and writing is still marked individually. Speaking does not share: Criterion C depends on time spent talking, a shared hour halves it, and in practice one student dominates so the quieter one gets less than half. Where the two students are two or more phases apart we decline the pair, since the session is then pitched wrongly for at least one of them.

faqs.question: Why does Phase 5 French cost more than Phase 2 in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Supply. Dubai has a large francophone population and two French-system schools, so fluent speakers who can teach beginner and middle-phase French are plentiful and the lower bands stay competitive. Teachers who can work on Phase 5 and 6 register, analytical vocabulary and unadapted text are mostly employed by schools, and the private pool is small. The cost curve across the phases is therefore flat at the bottom and steep at the top, which is not how parents expect pricing to behave.

faqs.question: Is marking included in a French tutoring rate?
faqs.answer: With us it is, and it is the question worth asking every provider first. An hour of teaching and an hour that includes setting a written task, banding it against the phase descriptor and returning it before the next session are different products often advertised at similar prices. Ask whether marking is inside the figure and what the turnaround is. Once both quotes answer that, they become comparable, and the apparently cheaper one frequently is not cheaper at all.

faqs.question: Do French rates in Dubai go up before report cards?
faqs.answer: Headline rates often stay still while effective prices rise, because the specialist end books out first and what remains is whatever is left. A family looking three weeks before an internal assessment or a reporting window is choosing from a thinner pool at whatever that pool asks. Starting a block mid-term, when diaries are open, is the nearest thing to a free saving in this market. Our rate is fixed for the term in which it is agreed and is not re-quoted as a deadline approaches.

faqs.question: Are the AED figures on this page inclusive of tax?
faqs.answer: The figures on this page are other providers' published market rates, so what they include is a question for each of them. For our own quotes we state plainly whether the figure is inclusive of any applicable tax before anything is agreed. We deliberately do not characterise the UAE tax treatment of tuition in general, because that requires a Federal Tax Authority source and is not something any family should take from a tutoring page. Ask every provider to confirm what will actually leave your account.

faqs.question: What are the hidden extras in a French tutoring package?
faqs.answer: Four recur. Marking charged separately after an hourly rate has been agreed. Required materials, which for MYP French should be minimal because the work is the student's own school tasks plus authentic text. Cancellation terms, where the question is how much notice avoids a charge and whether a missed session can be deferred inside a block. And tax treatment of the quoted figure. All four are avoidable by asking before booking rather than during the first disagreement about an invoice.

faqs.question: Is a holiday intensive cheaper than a term of weekly French?
faqs.answer: Cheaper in total and more expensive per hour, and it suits a narrow purpose. Daily sessions across one or two weeks of a Dubai school break can close a named gap quickly, which makes it a good purchase before French B starts in Year 12. Published specialist bands put a two-week intensive at roughly AED 2,000 to 4,500. The gains fade without some term-time follow-up, so budget a few sessions after it at the same moment rather than finding out in October.

faqs.question: How do we avoid paying a tutor to work out what the problem is?
faqs.answer: Send the evidence before the first session: a page of your child's own written French, the latest report with its criterion bands if the school prints them, and where they were schooled before Dubai. Then insist the first session ends with a written phase estimate, a named target criterion and a band on marked work. That turns a diagnosis into a forty-minute job rather than four paid sessions of orientation, and the note stays useful for a year even if you book nothing else.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to start French support in MYP 3 or wait until MYP 5?
faqs.answer: MYP 3 is cheaper per hour, cheaper in total and more effective, which is an unusual combination. Early and middle-phase work sits in the lower market bands, habits are still forming, and the same gap takes fewer hours to close. By MYP 5 the work is in the specialist band, the record that decides the Diploma route is already largely written, and the family is buying under time pressure. Waiting almost always costs more and buys a narrower set of options at the end of it.

faqs.question: If we are offered a cheaper French tutor instead, what are we losing?
faqs.answer: Ask what specifically changes, because sometimes the answer is nothing that matters. A budget-band tutor for Phase 1 or 2 vocabulary work is good value and specialist rates there are waste. What a lower rate usually removes is marking, assessment experience against phase descriptors, and the ability to say what the next band requires. For a student losing marks on written register, those three are the entire product. Have them band a script before deciding; the answer makes the trade-off obvious in five minutes.

dubai/ib-myp-french-home-tutor.closingHeading: Decide the criterion, then the price makes sense
dubai/ib-myp-french-home-tutor.closingBody: Almost every confusing French quote in Dubai becomes clear once five things are written down: the phase, whether marking is included, the minimum session length, the frequency, and whether anybody is travelling. Work those out and two numbers that looked incomparable differ in two specific places you can then judge. Send the last report and a page of your child's written French; the first session is free and ends with a phase estimate, a target criterion and a band on marked work, which you keep whatever you decide. Our quote follows, with marking inside it. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not sell home visits in Dubai.

dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach MYP French at the phase a school has actually placed a student in, and they count errors rather than describing them. Send the last report with its criterion bands if the school prints them, plus one piece of your child's own written French.

intro.heading: A 5 in MYP French can mean two opposite problems
paragraphs: Dubai produces an unusual mix of French students, and it is the reason generic French tutoring so often fails here. Two French-system schools feed the city, a large francophone professional population lives in it, and a great many international schools timetable French as a standard Language Acquisition option. The result is that one MYP French classroom can hold a student who has been educated in French since the age of three sitting next to one who learned the numbers last year.

The MYP handles that with phases. French runs across six of them, and a phase describes what a student can do with the language rather than how long they have studied it. Each phase has its own descriptors, and the four criteria, listening, reading, speaking and writing, are each marked on a band out of eight against those descriptors. A grade therefore means nothing on its own. A 5 in Phase 2 and a 5 in Phase 5 describe entirely different students with entirely different problems.

The two problems are almost mirror images. The French-system arrival has fluency, instinct and idiom, and loses marks on text type, register and the accuracy that decays once a child stops writing in French daily. The English-medium learner has explicit rules, neat conjugation tables and exam habits, and loses marks on listening speed and on speaking when nothing has been rehearsed. Teaching either of them as though they were the other wastes a term and frustrates everybody involved.

Separating them takes marked evidence rather than conversation. A fluent student's writing shows agreement errors appearing exactly where attention lapses. A rule-learner's writing is accurate and thin, with one tense doing all the work. Both of those are visible on a single page of written French to somebody who knows what to look for, which is why the first session on this page is a diagnosis and the first thing produced is a band with a reason attached.

What follows is the detail: how phase placement usually falls for each kind of Dubai arrival, which grammar points start costing marks at which phase, why listening defeats children who speak French at home, and how counting one error type across four dated scripts tells you whether a rule has genuinely landed. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai.

One thing is deliberately absent from the pages that rank for this search, and it is the reason this one is long. Nobody publishes the order in which French grammar starts costing marks, nobody sets out how placement actually falls for a child leaving the French system, and nobody explains why a francophone household can be handed a middling grade. Those three questions account for most of what a Dubai parent is really asking when they type the name of this subject into a search box, so they are answered here with tables rather than reassurance.

Two mirror-image profiles: fluent and inaccurate, or accurate and inflexible

dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.programmesIntro: French appears at every stage of an IB school career in Dubai, and the decision points are not evenly spaced. Two of them matter more than the rest: the phase a student is placed in on arrival, and the Group 2 route chosen at the end of MYP 5.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: French sits in Language Acquisition with six phases and four criteria. Assessment is continuous, so a weak term is carried rather than resat, and the grade is a judgement against descriptors rather than an average of test scores. The phase assigned on arrival often persists for years, which makes it the most consequential decision in the subject and the one parents are least often consulted about.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's mobility makes phase mismatches frequent. Families arrive mid-year from Lyon, Casablanca, Abidjan or Montreal, sit a forty-minute placement test in their first week, and get a phase. A student who should be in Phase 5 and lands in Phase 3 will coast for two years and then find Higher Level French closed to them at exactly the moment it matters.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: French in the primary years is reported narratively with no bands, and the amount timetabled varies enormously between schools. Thirty minutes a week and three lessons a week both appear on a report as French, which is why two children can arrive in MYP 1 looking identical on paper and be two phases apart in a classroom.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families moving a child between schools at Year 6 should ask the receiving school which phase its MYP 1 French cohort starts from, and whether a child with limited primary French will be placed below it. The answer determines whether MYP 1 is a continuation or a standing start, and schools differ considerably on this.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: French becomes Group 2: French B at Standard or Higher Level, French ab initio for a genuine beginner, or French A where a school offers the literature route. Schools check prior study before allowing ab initio, so a student who took French throughout the MYP will not be permitted onto the beginner course however weak their marks were.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP 5 record is what Dubai schools use to allocate these routes, and option blocks are built a year ahead. A Phase 4 student with consistent upper-band marks is a credible Higher Level candidate; the same student with mid-band reading usually gets Standard Level. Raise the question during MYP 4, because by the spring of MYP 5 the timetable has already decided.

dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.subjectsIntro: French bookings here are made against a specific fault rather than against the subject as a whole, because the two common Dubai profiles need almost opposite work. Each item below is something that shows up in marked writing or a recorded oral, and can be counted.

subjects.name: Noun gender and article agreement
subjects.description: The most countable error in early French writing and the one that compounds, because gender drives adjective and participle agreement later. The fix is habit rather than theory: nouns learned with the article attached, never alone, and a proofreading pass that looks only at articles.

subjects.name: Perfect against imperfect
subjects.description: Where narrative writing is won and lost. The classic error is a whole story told in one past tense. Measured by counting tense choices in a short narrative, then having the student write the same story twice, once in each tense, before mixing them deliberately.

subjects.name: Adjective and past-participle agreement
subjects.description: Fluent students fail this precisely where they stop paying attention, which makes the error distribution across a page diagnostic in itself. A dedicated proofreading pass that ignores everything except agreement usually removes most of it within a month.

subjects.name: Pronoun order and placement
subjects.description: Students avoid the problem rather than make errors, dropping pronouns in speech so the sentence stays safe. That avoidance shows as repetitive, flat speaking in Criterion C. Substitution drills on three fixed frames restore it faster than explanation does.

subjects.name: The subjunctive after fixed triggers
subjects.description: Not a grammar curiosity but a band ceiling, because avoiding it flattens register in exactly the pieces where register carries marks. Five trigger phrases learned properly and used deliberately in every written task is the whole of the early work.

subjects.name: Listening: numbers, liaison and elision
subjects.description: The specific reason children who speak French at home lose Criterion A marks. Measured by logging which question types fail rather than by playing more audio, because numbers, negatives and speaker attitude fail for entirely different reasons.

subjects.name: Text types for Criterion D
subjects.description: Letters, blog entries, reports, interviews, each with its own conventions and register. The most common wasted marks in the subject belong here: an excellent piece of writing answering a different task than the one set.

subjects.name: Oral: unprepared turns and visual stimulus
subjects.description: Rehearsed answers sound excellent for ninety seconds and then run out, which is the standard Criterion C failure. Three-minute unprepared turns, recorded with consent and played back, builds recovery after an error rather than polish before one.

subjects.name: Phase placement evidence for French-system arrivals
subjects.description: Three tasks across the four criteria banded against both the assigned phase and the one above, written up for a coordinator. Used most often by families whose child was placed from a short entry test on a jet-lagged week.

dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.regionsIntro: French demand in Dubai clusters around the francophone professional communities and around the schools that receive students leaving the French system. These are the areas bookings come from most, with the timing or placement pattern that recurs in each.

regions.name: Al Sufouh and Knowledge Village
regions.note: Close to several international schools and to a francophone working population, so arrival times are early and 4pm slots hold. A high share of requests here concern students placed below where their spoken French sits.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim and Al Manara
regions.note: Established villa communities with children spread across IB and British schools. Bookings here are typically middle-phase, with writing accuracy rather than fluency as the target criterion.

regions.name: The Springs and The Lakes
regions.note: Family communities with long activity calendars. The pattern that survives a term is two short slots on fixed weekdays, because a single long session is the first thing traded away when a fixture appears.

regions.name: Al Garhoud and Dubai Festival City
regions.note: Near the eastern school cluster, with shorter commutes than most of the city. Requests from here skew towards students who moved out of the French system two or three years ago and whose written accuracy has quietly decayed.

regions.name: Jumeirah Beach Residence
regions.note: Apartment living where the constraint is a quiet room rather than a drive. Thirty-minute oral slots work better here than long evening sessions, and headphones solve most of what parents worry about.

regions.name: Dubai Land and Liwan
regions.note: Long bus runs in both directions push realistic start times past 5.30pm. Written tasks tend to be done at the weekend, which suits the error-tally approach because the scripts arrive in a predictable rhythm.

regions.name: Arjan and Al Barsha South
regions.note: Newer communities feeding several IB schools nearby. Mixed-phase French classes are common in this cluster, which raises the value of one-to-one work because a mixed class cannot pitch at any single phase.

sections.heading: What an IB MYP French tutor in Dubai fixes first
paragraphs: The first session produces a diagnosis, and the diagnosis is almost always one of two things. Either the student has fluency without accuracy, which shows as writing that reads well and loses marks in predictable places, or they have accuracy without flexibility, which shows as neat short sentences and a recorded oral that stops after ninety seconds. Those two need different work, different session shapes and different lengths of time, and confusing them is the standard failure in Dubai French tutoring.

Telling them apart takes one page of the student's own written French and three minutes of unprepared speech. The fluent profile shows agreement errors clustered where attention lapsed, idiom used confidently, and register that drifts from formal to conversational mid-piece. The rule-learner's page is accurate, short, and built on one tense doing all the work, with no idiom at all. Both produce a middling band. Only one of them is a grammar problem.

What happens next follows from that. A fluent student gets text types, register and a dedicated proofreading pass, because their language is already there and the marks are being lost to assessment conventions. A rule-learner gets frequency: short oral slots, listening logs, and permission to be inaccurate while being flexible. The common mistake is to give both of them more grammar worksheets, which helps one of them slightly and the other not at all.

The output of the first session is written down: the phase estimate, the profile, one target error type, and the band on the piece of work that was marked. That note is worth keeping even if no further lessons are booked, because it is a sentence a parent can take to a subject teacher and get a real answer to, rather than a general worry that produces a general reassurance.

sections.heading: Phase placement for children arriving from the French system
paragraphs: Dubai schools place students into French phases from an entry assessment, usually in the first week, usually short, and often sat by a child who arrived in the country ten days earlier. For most students that works out roughly right. For children leaving the French system it frequently does not, because an entry test that samples reading and writing catches a student whose strengths are oral and whose written French has not been exercised since they changed schools.

The table sets out how placement usually falls for the main Dubai arrival routes, along with the gap each profile carries and a planning estimate for closing it. Treat the week ranges as planning figures rather than promises: they assume a weekly session with written work in between, and a student doing twice-weekly short slots on a narrow target moves faster. The point of the table is the pattern, which is that the gap is predictable once you know where a child came from.

The most commonly disputed row is the francophone home with no French schooling. These students speak and understand far above their phase and read and write far below it, so any single placement number is wrong in two directions at once. Schools tend to place on the written evidence, which feels unfair to the family and is defensible from the school's side, because the written criteria are half the marks and the student genuinely cannot access the upper phase in two of four criteria.

If you want a placement reconsidered, the route is documentary rather than argumentative. Collect three recent marked tasks across the four criteria, have them banded against both the assigned phase and the one above, and send one page to the coordinator. A written request gets a written answer and survives a change of teacher in August, which a conversation at a parents' evening does not.

sections.heading: French grammar in the order it starts costing marks
paragraphs: Textbooks teach grammar in the order a linguist would arrange it. Marks are lost in a different order entirely, and tutoring that follows the textbook spends weeks on things that are not currently costing anything. The sequence below is ordered by the phase at which each point begins to affect a band, which means it is also roughly the order in which a Dubai MYP student should be made to care about it.

Gender comes first and is the most under-rated, because it compounds. A student who defaults to masculine on unfamiliar nouns will go on to make every adjective and participle agreement error downstream of that choice, and the errors will look like agreement problems when the cause sits one step earlier. Learning nouns with the article attached is dull, unfashionable advice and it removes a whole class of later error.

At the other end, the subjunctive is not a refinement. From Phase 5 it becomes a band ceiling, because the pieces where it belongs are the pieces where register carries marks, and a student who avoids it writes in a flattened register that cannot reach the upper bands. Five trigger phrases, learned properly and used deliberately in every written task for a month, is the whole of the early work and it is far less daunting than the grammar books make it look.

One warning about the middle of the table. Agreement and tense choice are the two points where fluent students and rule-learners look most different. The fluent student makes errors where attention lapses, so the mistakes cluster in the second half of a page. The rule-learner makes no mistakes and also takes no risks, so the page is accurate and thin. The same table entry therefore implies opposite work depending on which profile is in front of you.

sections.heading: Listening: why a child who speaks French at home still drops marks
paragraphs: This is the result that convinces francophone parents something has gone wrong with the marking. A child who argues with their grandmother in French every Sunday scores six out of eight on Criterion A, and the conclusion drawn is that the test is unfair or the teacher is harsh. Usually neither is true. Assessed listening asks for things that conversation never does, and a lifetime of conversation does not practise any of them.

Three failure types account for most of it. Numbers, because spoken French numbers between sixty and a hundred are constructed arithmetically and a listener who hesitates has already missed the next clause. Negatives, because the negative particle is frequently reduced or dropped in speech and a listener following the gist takes the positive meaning. And speaker attitude, which asks a student to infer irony or reluctance from tone, a skill nobody acquires by chatting to family.

The useful intervention is a log rather than more audio. Each failed question is tagged by type, and over six weeks the pattern is obvious: a student who misses every number question and nothing else has a completely different problem from one who misses every inference question. More listening practice helps both of them slowly. Targeted work on the failing type helps one of them quickly, and the log is what tells you which.

Replaying with the transcript revealed afterwards is the mechanism that makes this stick. The student answers under timed conditions, then sees exactly where comprehension broke and hears the same clip again knowing what was said. Over several weeks the number of question types in the failure column falls, and that count is the evidence a family can read without listening to a word of French themselves.

sections.heading: The error tally: how four marked scripts prove a rule has landed
paragraphs: Grammar is explained in one session and learned over many, and the gap between those two facts is where most tutoring money disappears. A student nods, understands perfectly, and makes the identical error the following week, which is normal and is not a sign that the explanation failed. What is needed is a way of telling the difference between understood, practised and automatic, because those three states need completely different amounts of further work.

Counting one error type across four dated scripts does that. Script one establishes the baseline on the target error and nothing else is counted, so the number is clean. Script two, a week later on a different task, shows whether the rule survives a change of context. Script three is the student's own rewrite, which tests whether they can find the error unaided rather than recognise it when pointed out. Script four is written under time pressure, which is where automatic and merely known diverge.

The last row of the table matters most and is the one families find counter-intuitive. Error counts can fall while the Criterion D band stays still, and that is informative rather than disappointing. It means the grammar work succeeded and the band is being held down by something else, almost always text type or register. Without the count you cannot tell the difference between a failed intervention and a successful one that revealed the next problem.

One practical note. Count one error type at a time and count it the same way every week, including the obvious instances. The temptation is to count everything, which produces a number too noisy to compare, or to stop counting the instances a student has clearly mastered, which quietly flatters the trend. Boring consistency is what makes four scripts into evidence rather than four impressions.

sections.heading: MYP French and DELF are two different things
paragraphs: Dubai families often hold a DELF certificate and assume it maps onto a phase, or ask whether tutoring for one covers the other. It does not map cleanly. DELF is a separate external qualification in French as a foreign language, assessed on its own levels and sat in its own sessions. MYP French is assessed internally against phase descriptors, on four criteria, by the school, with moderation. Different awarding body, different assessment design, different purpose.

There is useful overlap in skills and almost none in conventions. A student preparing for DELF practises task formats that do not appear in MYP assessment, and an MYP student writes to text type and register requirements that DELF frames differently. A certificate is good evidence that a student can function at a level, and it is poor evidence of which phase they belong in, because the school is marking against its own descriptors rather than against an external scale.

Where a DELF certificate genuinely helps is in a placement conversation, as one piece of evidence among several rather than as a trump card. A coordinator presented with a certificate and three recent marked tasks banded against two phases has something to work with. A coordinator presented with only a certificate has a document from a different system and no information about how the student performs on the tasks their own school sets.

If a family wants both, say so early, because the preparation is additive rather than shared. Running MYP work and DELF preparation inside one weekly hour generally produces a thin version of each. The honest options are to prioritise one for a term, or to accept that two targets means more hours, and that is a budget conversation rather than a teaching one.

sections.heading: Where French sits in a Dubai timetable alongside mandatory Arabic
paragraphs: French is a choice; Arabic in a Dubai private school is not. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are mandatory in every Dubai private school regardless of the licensed curriculum, and KHDA guidance requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, stating that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because expectations and the language of instruction differ.

For a non-Arab MYP student choosing French, that means two languages running simultaneously, one of which uses an unfamiliar script. This is the single most common source of language fatigue in Dubai MYP cohorts, and it is worth naming when a family is deciding how many paid hours to buy. Adding a third weekly language session to a child already carrying two unfamiliar languages is frequently counter-productive, whatever the grades suggest.

The timetable arithmetic is worth checking too. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time from a 40-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and advises that no mandatory subject lesson runs shorter than 25 minutes. Those units come out of a finite week, which is why some schools offer a narrower Language Acquisition menu than parents expect and why French is occasionally dropped as an option in a particular year group.

The practical advice is to sequence rather than stack. If both French and Arabic need support, run one as a short focused block while the other sits on school provision alone, then swap. Two half-hearted weekly sessions in two languages tends to produce two unchanged bands, while one properly targeted block usually produces one that has moved and a student who still has some appetite left.

sections.heading: Phase 5, Phase 6 and the Diploma French decision
paragraphs: The end of MYP 5 is where French stops being a school subject and starts being a university input, and Dubai schools apply the rules fairly tightly. French B Higher Level normally goes to students finishing in Phase 4 or above with consistent upper-band marks. Standard Level covers most of the rest. French ab initio is reserved for genuine beginners, and a student who studied French throughout the MYP will not be admitted to it whatever their marks looked like.

The lever in MYP 5 is usually Criterion B or Criterion D, because reading and writing are what a school examines when deciding whether a student can handle Higher Level text work. A student with strong speaking and mid-band reading is the classic Standard Level allocation that could have been Higher Level with a term of targeted reading work in the right year. The right year is MYP 4 into early MYP 5, not the spring.

For Phase 6 students, and for some bilingual students whose school agrees, the other route is French A, where the language is studied as literature. That is a different subject with different assessment and a different kind of work, and in Dubai it comes up most often for students out of the French system. It is also a timetable question: option blocks for Year 12 are built a year ahead, so a request made in May for a September start is usually too late.

The conversation to have, in MYP 4, is specific rather than general. Ask the Diploma coordinator which phase and which criterion profile they would want to see for Higher Level, and ask the French teacher where your child currently sits against that. Two answers, written down, turn a vague worry about options into a target that a term of work can actually address.

sections.heading: When the household speaks French and the grade is still a 5
paragraphs: This is the most frequent and most frustrating call we take about French in Dubai. The family speaks French at home, the child is genuinely fluent, and the MYP report says 5. Parents reasonably conclude that something is broken, and the usual suspicion falls on the teacher. In almost every case the explanation is structural: fluency is being measured against descriptors that reward things conversation never asks for, and the student has never been taught those things.

Look at where the marks actually sit. Criterion C speaking is probably already strong, and Criterion A listening is often respectable. The losses are concentrated in Criterion B reading, where unadapted text and inference questions are a different skill from understanding speech, and in Criterion D writing, where text type, register and written accuracy carry the band. Half the marks in the subject live in those two criteria, which is why speaking well cannot carry a grade.

The work is therefore narrow and it is not really French teaching. It is assessment literacy: what a formal letter requires that a spoken explanation does not, how register is signalled in writing, how to keep a register consistent for a whole page, and how to run a proofreading pass for agreement when the language feels automatic. Most fluent students move a band or two on this within a term because the language was never the problem.

One further possibility is worth checking before buying any hours: the phase itself. A fluent student placed in Phase 3 can be scoring highly against Phase 3 descriptors and still receive a middling grade if the school converts from a wider set. Ask for the four criterion bands and the phase in writing. Occasionally the right answer is a phase conversation rather than tutoring at all, and that answer costs nothing.

process.title: Send a page of written French and the last report
process.description: One piece of your child's own written French tells an experienced teacher which of the two profiles you have, which is the thing that decides everything else. Add the report with its criterion bands if the school prints them, and say where your child was schooled before Dubai.

process.title: Free first session that ends with a band and a reason
process.description: Sixty minutes covering a short reading, three minutes of unprepared speech, a listening task and a piece of writing. It finishes with a phase estimate, the profile, one target error type and a band on the marked work. You keep the note whatever you decide afterwards, and no card is taken.

process.title: Agree the target and the counting rule
process.description: One error type, counted the same way on every script, reported weekly alongside the band. We also agree the session shape: a weekly hour for writing work, or two short slots for oral and listening. Dubai slots run from 4pm to 7pm on weekdays with weekend mornings available.

process.title: Review after the fourth script
process.description: Four dated scripts is the point at which a count means something. If it has fallen and the band has moved, we pick the next target. If the count fell and the band did not, the problem is text type or register and we say so. If nothing moved, we change the method or the tutor.

whyPoints.title: The profile before the grammar
whyPoints.description: Fluent-and-inaccurate and accurate-and-inflexible are opposite problems that produce the same middling band. We name which one you have from marked work in the first hour, because every decision after that depends on the answer.

whyPoints.title: Errors counted, not described
whyPoints.description: One target error type, counted identically on four dated scripts, including the obvious instances. A count can be compared with last week. A comment saying agreement is improving cannot, and it is the most common thing a family is given instead.

whyPoints.title: Grammar in mark-losing order
whyPoints.description: Gender and article agreement before the subjunctive, because the first compounds into everything downstream and the second only starts costing marks from Phase 5. Textbook order and mark-losing order are not the same sequence, and only one of them is worth paying for.

whyPoints.title: Honest about Arabic running alongside
whyPoints.description: A non-Arab student taking French in Dubai is carrying two unfamiliar languages, one in another script. We will advise sequencing blocks rather than stacking weekly sessions, even where that means selling fewer hours this term.

whyPoints.title: Phase specialists from anywhere in the country
whyPoints.description: Because lessons run over live video, a Phase 5 or Phase 6 French specialist is reachable whatever community you live in. That matters because the upper phases are the thinnest part of the Dubai French market and the part a postcode search is least likely to find.

faqs.question: What does an MYP French tutor work on in the first few sessions?
faqs.answer: Diagnosis, then one narrow target. The first session establishes which of the two common Dubai profiles your child has: fluent but inaccurate, or accurate but inflexible. Those are opposite problems that produce similar grades and need almost opposite teaching. From the second session the work is one target error type, or one criterion, with written work set and marked every week. You should finish the first month holding a phase estimate, a named profile, and at least two dated scripts with bands and error counts on them.

faqs.question: My child came from a French-system school. Which MYP phase will they be placed in?
faqs.answer: Usually Phase 5 or 6 if they completed the French curriculum, and Phase 4 if they moved into English-medium schooling a couple of years ago and their written accuracy has decayed since. Placement comes from a short entry test in the first week, which samples reading and writing and therefore under-reads oral strength. If the assigned phase looks wrong, collect three recent marked tasks, have them banded against the assigned phase and the one above, and put the request to the coordinator in writing.

faqs.question: Which French grammar errors cost the most marks in the MYP?
faqs.answer: In order of when they start to matter: noun gender and article agreement from Phase 1, present-tense endings under speaking pressure from Phase 2, the perfect against the imperfect from Phase 3, adjective and participle agreement from Phases 3 to 4, pronoun placement from Phase 4, and the subjunctive from Phase 5. Gender is the most under-rated because it compounds into every later agreement error. The subjunctive is not a refinement; avoiding it flattens register in exactly the pieces where register carries the band.

faqs.question: Why does my child understand French at home but lose marks on listening tasks?
faqs.answer: Because assessed listening asks for things conversation never does. Three types account for most losses: numbers, since spoken French numbers above sixty are constructed arithmetically and a hesitation costs the next clause; negatives, which are often reduced in speech so a gist-listener takes the positive meaning; and speaker attitude, which requires inferring irony or reluctance from tone. The fix is a log of which question types fail rather than more listening, because each type fails for a different reason and needs different work.

faqs.question: How do we know a French grammar rule has actually landed?
faqs.answer: Count one error type across four dated scripts. The baseline script gives the number to beat. A second script a week later on a different task shows whether the rule survives a change of context. The third is the student's own rewrite, testing whether they can find the error unaided. The fourth is written under time pressure, which is where automatic and merely known diverge. Count the same way every week including the obvious instances, or the trend quietly flatters itself.

faqs.question: Is MYP French the same as DELF?
faqs.answer: No. DELF is an external qualification in French as a foreign language with its own levels and sessions. MYP French is assessed internally by the school against phase descriptors on four criteria, with moderation. The skills overlap considerably and the conventions barely at all, so preparing for one does not cover the other. A DELF certificate is useful evidence in a placement conversation alongside recent marked work, and poor evidence on its own, because it says nothing about performance on the tasks your child's school actually sets.

faqs.question: Does my child still take Arabic if they choose French in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Yes. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are mandatory in every Dubai private school whatever curriculum is licensed, so French is a choice taken in addition rather than instead. For a non-Arab student that means two unfamiliar languages at once, one in a different script, which is the most common source of language fatigue in Dubai MYP cohorts. If both need support, sequence them as separate focused blocks rather than running two weekly sessions in parallel and getting a thin version of each.

faqs.question: Our household speaks French and the MYP grade is still a 5. Why?
faqs.answer: Because half the marks sit in reading and writing, and fluency does not deliver those. Criterion C speaking is probably already strong and Criterion A respectable. The losses concentrate in Criterion B, where unadapted text and inference are a different skill from understanding speech, and Criterion D, where text type, register and written accuracy carry the band. The work needed is assessment literacy rather than French teaching, and most fluent students move a band or two within a term once somebody explains what the descriptors are actually asking for.

faqs.question: When does the subjunctive start to matter in MYP French?
faqs.answer: From Phase 5, and then it matters a great deal. Below that it is a curiosity. From Phase 5 the written tasks that attract the upper bands are the ones where register has to be controlled, and a student who avoids the subjunctive writes in a flattened register that cannot reach those bands however accurate everything else is. The practical starting point is five trigger phrases, learned properly and used deliberately in every piece of writing for a month, which is much less daunting than a grammar chapter.

faqs.question: How many MYP French sessions a week are sensible?
faqs.answer: One weekly hour with written work in between suits writing and reading targets, where the marking turnaround is what produces the gain. Two short slots a week suit speaking and listening, because fluency and comprehension speed respond to frequency rather than to length. More than two sessions a week in one language is rarely productive for an MYP student who is also carrying mandatory Arabic, and it tends to produce resentment before it produces a band.

faqs.question: What is the practical difference between Phase 4 and Phase 5 French?
faqs.answer: Phase 4 students discuss opinions, handle unfamiliar text with contextual support, and vary register in writing with prompting. Phase 5 students analyse and infer, work across several text types, and control tense and register without being told to. The jump is mostly in independence rather than in vocabulary. For Diploma purposes it is the difference that matters, because French B Higher Level normally goes to students finishing MYP 5 in Phase 4 or above with consistent upper-band marks.

faqs.question: Will MYP French get my child onto French B Higher Level?
faqs.answer: It depends on the MYP 5 phase and the criterion profile, and the decision is made by the school from its own records. Higher Level usually requires Phase 4 or above with consistent upper-band marks, particularly in reading and writing, because those are the criteria that predict whether a student can handle Higher Level text work. A student with strong speaking and mid-band reading is the classic Standard Level allocation. The time to change that is MYP 4 into early MYP 5, since option blocks are built a year ahead.

faqs.question: Can a tutor mark my child's French writing against the MYP criteria?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the main thing worth asking for. The useful format is the student's own piece of writing, the criterion letter, the band out of eight, two or three specific places in the text that put it in that band, and one sentence on what the next band requires. Alongside that, a count of the target error type. Anything vaguer cannot be compared with next month's version. What a tutor must not do is edit or rewrite work that will be submitted as the student's own.

faqs.question: Should we move our child from French to another language option?
faqs.answer: Rarely, and almost never in MYP 4 or 5. Switching resets the phase, loses the accumulated credit of several years, and usually produces a lower starting point than the grade that prompted the move. The exception is a student placed in a phase far above their actual level who is drowning, where a school may agree to a different option at a lower phase. Before considering it, ask for the four criterion bands and the phase in writing, because the problem is sometimes placement rather than the language.

faqs.question: What happens if no Phase 5 French tutor is free at our time?
faqs.answer: We say so rather than fill the hour. The upper phases are the thinnest part of this market and we are not exempt from that. What we will offer is a different weekday, a shorter twice-weekly pattern, or a tutor who is strong specifically in the criterion you need rather than across the whole phase, with the limitation stated plainly. What we will not do is put a fluent French speaker without MYP criterion experience into a Phase 5 slot and leave you to find out.

dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.closingHeading: Send one page of French and we will tell you which problem you have
dubai/ib-myp-french-tutor.closingBody: The quickest way to a useful answer is a photograph of a page of your child's own written French plus the latest report. From those two things an experienced MYP teacher can usually name the profile, the likely phase and the first target error type before a lesson has happened. The first session is free, ends with a band and a written reason for it, and is yours to keep whether or not anything follows. After that the evidence is a counted error type across four dated scripts. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Dubai.

dubai/ib-myp-home-tutor.tutorsIntro: The rate a family pays tracks scarcity and level, not distance. A Middle Years subject specialist costs less per hour than a Diploma Higher Level examiner-experienced tutor, and the tutors below are matched to the year group and subject group rather than to the biggest number on a price list.

intro.heading: The price question, answered in dirhams before anything else
paragraphs: Three of the six most visible tutoring sites serving Dubai publish no price at all. Two quote in US dollars. One contradicts its own figures between two pages. That is why a parent searching for an IB MYP home tutor in Dubai ends up on a form rather than on an answer, and it is why this page opens with numbers and their sources instead of with a description of our teaching philosophy.

The published market picture for Dubai in 2026 looks like this. Budget and university-student tutoring works out at roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. Qualified subject tutors working online sit at AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors publishing International GCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. In-home one-to-one visits, travel included, run from AED 180 to AED 500, with Bestimate's 2026 Dubai cost table putting the band at AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors quoting AED 200 to 500. Specialist IB and IGCSE teaching sits at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270, and premium named tutors reach AED 650, as BartyED publishes.

Those are market rates. They are not an IB Gram price list, and nobody should present a competitor's number as their own. What they establish is the shape of the market: the online and in-home bands overlap at the bottom and separate sharply at the top, and the gap between them is almost entirely the cost of a car.

Middle Years work sits lower in those bands than Diploma work, and it is worth understanding why rather than just enjoying it. There is no external examination in most years of the programme, no Higher Level content ceiling, and no internally assessed component carrying a published mark allocation in the way a Diploma internal assessment does. The teaching is about criterion writing, investigation design and process documentation, which a strong subject teacher can do without the examiner-level specialism that prices the top band.

The second half of the price question is what changes the number, and in Dubai the variables are specific. Year group, standard versus extended mathematics, whether the school runs the programme to Year 11 or switches to International GCSE, whether Arabic is a first or additional language stream, whether a Personal Project is in progress, how far a tutor would have to drive, and whether the slot sits in the peak 16:00 to 19:00 window that every family in the city wants. Each of those moves the rate, some by a little and one of them by a great deal.

This page works through all of it: the provider models compared with sources and dates, what travel really costs, the seven variables that move the rate, tutoring set against Dubai school fees and the 2026-27 fee freeze, how monthly packages actually arithmetic out, the permit question, and where families reliably waste money. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home tutoring is a service we run only in India, and every UAE lesson is one to one over live video.

dubai/ib-myp-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Spend across the five programme years is not flat. These are the four phases where families actually open their wallets, with what the money typically buys in each.

programmes.name: Middle Years 1 to 3 - the cheap window
programmes.description: The lowest-cost phase to buy support in, because there is no external assessment and the work is skill-building rather than examination preparation. A qualified subject tutor in the AED 150 to 300 published band is the right tier here, and a short block of six to eight sessions on one criterion is usually a complete intervention rather than the start of an open-ended commitment.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families overwhelmingly skip this phase and buy later at a higher rate. The arithmetic argues the other way: six sessions at the mid band costs less than a term of examination-year remediation, and the criteria being built here are the ones every later mark depends on. Spend early and small, not late and large.

programmes.name: Middle Years 4 and 5 - where the rate rises
programmes.description: Content depth increases, mathematics splits into standard and extended, sciences may separate into three subjects, and all four criteria are reported. Families typically move up a tier here, from the AED 150 to 300 band towards the AED 200 to 450 specialist band, and often buy two subjects rather than one. This is where an annual tuition budget is really set.
programmes.countryNote: The Dubai complication is the fork at sixteen. If the school switches the cohort to Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel International GCSE for Years 10 and 11, you are no longer buying criterion teaching at all; you are buying timed past-paper technique, which is priced differently and needs a different tutor. Confirm the route in writing before committing to a year.

programmes.name: Personal Project support - a block, not a subscription
programmes.description: Marked against three criteria - planning, applying skills and reflecting - each out of eight for a total of 24, and externally moderated. The honest commercial shape of this is a fortnightly block across the year rather than a weekly slot: perhaps twelve to sixteen sessions spread from the start of the project to submission, concentrated at the planning and reflection stages.
programmes.countryNote: The expensive mistake in Dubai is buying nothing until six weeks before submission and then buying a lot. Two of the three criteria are about process evidence recorded as it happened, which cannot be bought late at any price. A fortnightly slot from the start costs less in total and scores better.

programmes.name: The bridge into DP1 or International GCSE
programmes.description: A defined block over the summer and the first term of the new course, usually eight to twelve sessions in one or two subjects. The cost here is predictable because the scope is: closing the gap between what the programme assessed and what the next course assesses, which is a known list rather than an open-ended tutoring relationship.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai families who buy this block typically spend less across the following two years than those who do not, because the first-term grade shock is what triggers panic buying at the specialist rate. The block is cheaper than the panic, and the summer rate is not inflated by the peak-slot premium that applies in term time.

dubai/ib-myp-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Rate varies by subject as well as by level, and the reason is always supply. These are the subject streams Dubai families buy for Middle Years students, with what each one does to the price.

subjects.name: Mathematics, standard route
subjects.description: The most available subject in the city and therefore the one that prices at the bottom of the qualified-tutor band. Plenty of good teachers, high competition, and a criterion profile that is easy to diagnose from a single marked task.

subjects.name: Mathematics, extended route
subjects.description: Prices slightly above the standard route, because the investigation tasks carry less scaffolding and the tutor needs to be comfortable teaching pattern generalisation and justification rather than procedure. Still well inside the qualified-tutor band rather than the specialist one.

subjects.name: Integrated Sciences
subjects.description: Broad content across biology, chemistry and physics with the criterion load concentrated on investigation design and data processing. Widely available in Dubai, so it prices at the middle of the band and a short block usually suffices.

subjects.name: Biology, Chemistry and Physics as separate subjects
subjects.description: Once the sciences separate, a family is buying a subject specialist rather than a science teacher, and the rate rises accordingly. Buying all three at once is the single largest avoidable line on a Dubai tuition budget; one at a time, chosen by criterion profile, costs far less.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.description: Prices in the middle of the band with good availability. The work is analysing and producing text rather than content coverage, so sessions tend to be longer and fewer, which changes the monthly figure more than the hourly one.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition: French and Spanish
subjects.description: Availability in Dubai is reasonable and the rate sits mid-band, but phase placement is worth checking before paying anything. A student placed a phase too high looks weak when the real issue is placement, and that is a conversation with the school rather than a purchase.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: High demand across Dubai and mid-band pricing. A tutor works from the school's own material, because for the mandatory UAE subjects the use of different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is prohibited, which narrows the pool of tutors willing to work that way.

subjects.name: Arabic as a First Language
subjects.description: Prices towards the specialist band purely on scarcity. Standard Arabic grammar and literary analysis at first-language standard is a genuinely thin supply line in Dubai, and the rate reflects competition for a small group of qualified teachers.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Mid-band, with the entire price justification sitting in one criterion: thinking critically. Source evaluation by origin, purpose and limitation is the lowest-scoring strand in this subject group almost everywhere, and it is a defined teaching job.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Fewer tutors in Dubai are comfortable teaching the design cycle as an assessment rather than as a project, so availability is thinner and the rate drifts upward. Three of the four criteria live in the documentation, which is where the teaching value is.

subjects.name: Islamic Education and UAE Social Studies
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the international programme in Dubai private schools. Teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic are required to hold the appropriate approval from the Knowledge and Human Development Authority to teach those subjects, which is a credential worth asking about and which affects what support is available.

dubai/ib-myp-home-tutor.regionsTitle: Dubai communities and what the drive would have cost
dubai/ib-myp-home-tutor.regionsIntro: The in-home premium is a travel premium, and travel in Dubai is not evenly distributed. These are the communities where families most often ask us about home visits, with what a car-based lesson would really have involved from each.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches
regions.note: Spread-out villa community off Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed Road. A tutor coming from Jumeirah or Al Barsha at 17:00 is in traffic for forty minutes each way, and that hour and twenty minutes is in the rate whether the invoice names it or not.

regions.name: The Springs and The Meadows
regions.note: Interlinked villa communities with a single congested approach at peak. Short distances on a map and long journeys in practice, which is why in-home quotes to this area cluster at the upper end of the published band.

regions.name: Jumeirah Village Circle
regions.note: Dense apartment and townhouse community with notoriously slow internal circulation. Parking and finding the right building adds time on top of the drive, and tutors routinely price a minimum session length to make the trip viable.

regions.name: Motor City and Dubai Sports City
regions.note: Mid-city communities with reasonable access but heavy school-run congestion between 14:00 and 16:00. The 17:00 and 18:00 slots are the ones families want and the ones that cost most in any travel-based model.

regions.name: Town Square and Mudon
regions.note: Newer developments towards the southern edge of the city, where the distance from the established tutor base is real. In-home quotes here are the highest we hear about, and the gap against an online rate is at its widest.

regions.name: Damac Hills and Dubailand
regions.note: Villa communities set back from the main arteries, with long internal roads. A sixty-minute lesson here can mean a two-hour commitment for the tutor, which is why ninety-minute minimums are common in car-based quotes.

regions.name: Al Furjan and Discovery Gardens
regions.note: Well connected by road and metro but a long way from the northern school belt. Families here are often the first to do the arithmetic and conclude that the travel premium buys nothing academic.

regions.name: The Sustainable City and Remraam
regions.note: Southern communities where the local tutor pool is genuinely small. The choice is rarely between a good local visit and a good online lesson; it is between a long drive at a premium and a specialist on screen.

schoolClusters.city: Arabian Ranches, Motor City and Al Khail
schoolClusters.note: Continuum and British-curriculum campuses serving the central villa belt. Families here most often ask about in-home visits, and are the ones for whom the travel arithmetic is most lopsided given the peak-hour approach roads.
schools: Jumeirah English Speaking School, Arabian Ranches

schoolClusters.city: Jumeirah Village Circle and Al Furjan
schoolClusters.note: Dense, fast-growing communities with newer campuses and a young year-group profile, so Middle Years 1 to 3 requests dominate. Short distances and slow internal roads make the travel premium hard to justify here.

schoolClusters.city: Dubailand, Town Square and The Sustainable City
schoolClusters.note: The southern expansion, where the distance from the established tutor base is largest and online delivery changes the available choice rather than only the price. Several continuum campuses sit in this belt.

sections.heading: What an IB MYP home tutor in Dubai costs, and what we actually sell
paragraphs: The direct answer, in dirhams. Published Dubai market rates put an in-home one-to-one hourly visit at AED 180 to AED 500 with travel included, against AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified subject tutor working online and AED 200 to AED 450 and above for an IB or IGCSE specialist. Monthly packages seen in this market run at AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits. Those figures come from published competitor pages and from Bestimate's 2026 Dubai tutoring cost table, not from us.

The honest second half of that answer: IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai. There is no tutor who will arrive at a villa in Arabian Ranches or an apartment in Jumeirah Village Circle, and no UAE office or centre either. Home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one student with one tutor over live video, and we state that before a parent spends anything rather than after.

We still target the phrase, because it is the phrase Dubai parents type, and because the price comparison is the most useful thing anybody can give them. A family weighing AED 250 an hour for someone to drive to Town Square against AED 220 an hour for a subject specialist on screen is making a real decision, and the decision deserves actual numbers rather than a form.

What the premium buys is worth saying precisely. It buys presence in the room, which genuinely helps some younger students and some students with specific additional needs. It does not buy better subject knowledge, a wider choice of tutor, or more teaching minutes, and in the peak 17:00 to 19:00 window in Dubai it buys a meaningfully higher chance of a late or cancelled lesson. The tables below set that out line by line.

sections.heading: The Dubai market compared by provider model, with sources
paragraphs: Every competitor comparison table in this market measures itself against an unnamed straw man called other platforms. A useful version compares provider models instead, names what each one actually does, and quotes a rate only where the provider published it, with the source attached. That is what the table below does.

The pattern it reveals is consistent. Tuition centres and group classes are the cheapest per student and the least targeted, because a class of six cannot be taught to one child's criterion profile. Independent freelance tutors found through community groups are cheap and entirely unverified, including on the permit question. Agencies and platforms sit in the middle on price and vary enormously on whether they will replace a tutor who is not working. Premium named tutors reach AED 650 an hour and are worth it for a narrow set of final-year Diploma situations and almost never for Middle Years work.

The column most parents ignore and should not is the replacement policy. The largest wasted spend in Dubai tutoring is not a high hourly rate; it is six weeks of lessons with a tutor who was never the right match, paid in full because there was no mechanism to change. A provider that will swap the tutor on request after a bad first fortnight is worth more than one charging AED 40 an hour less.

One note on comparison honesty. Rates below are quoted with the provider and the date of the published figure, and no claim is made about anybody's quality or legality. Competitor pricing moves, and a figure published in 2026 should be checked against the provider's live page before a family relies on it.
