dubai/ib-myp-personal-project-home-tutor.programmesIntro: Project evidence looks different at each stage of the programme, and so does what a family can reasonably expect to see. These are the stages we cover for Dubai students, framed by what each one actually produces on paper.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme, Year 10
programmes.description: The year before the project, and the year the habits either form or do not. Subject teachers are marking against four criteria per group, so there is already criterion-referenced feedback in the house. Reading it with your child is free and tells you more about their self-management than any tutor's first impression will.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools vary in how much criterion feedback reaches parents. Some publish strand-level comments in the portal; others report a single number out of eight per criterion. If yours is the second kind, ask the form tutor for one piece of marked work with the strand commentary attached before you buy any outside help.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme, Year 11
programmes.description: Project year, running alongside the heaviest subject assessment of the programme and, at some schools, end-of-programme eAssessment. Evidence here is competing for the student's time with everything else, so the artefacts that matter are small and frequent rather than large and occasional.
programmes.countryNote: Many Dubai schools place the project report deadline between December and February, in the same window as internal mock examinations. That overlap is the practical reason evidence has to be checked fortnightly: a three-week silence in that term is not a pause, it is usually the project stopping.

programmes.name: The Personal Project
programmes.description: Three criteria, each marked 0 to 8, assessed on a report supported by a process journal. The product is evidence rather than a graded object. Everything a family can check between now and submission is either a journal entry, a plan revision, a product test or a draft paragraph.
programmes.countryNote: Confirm the criterion wording, the report format and the submission date with your child's Dubai MYP coordinator. Schools apply the current project guide and the detail has been revised, so a figure from a tutoring site is not a substitute for your school's own booklet.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme, first year
programmes.description: Where project habits either pay off or have to be rebuilt. The Extended Essay assumes a student can hold a question for months and keep a source record, and internal assessments in each subject assume the same discipline on a shorter cycle.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai students arriving in DP1 from a project treated as a January scramble tend to need the research-question work done again inside the first Extended Essay term. A short bridge block immediately after project submission is cheaper and lands better than a rescue a year later.

dubai/ib-myp-personal-project-home-tutor.subjectsIntro: Evidence looks different in each MYP subject group, because the skills a project borrows differ. These are the areas Dubai families most often pair with project coaching, described by the artefact each one should be producing.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: The evidence is iteration: sketched alternatives, a written specification, a tested prototype, a record of what failed. A Design-rooted project with one final photograph and no failed version in the folder is an evidence problem, not a talent problem, and it is visible from the first session.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Look for a control, a repeat and a numbers table with units. Students collect one data set and stop. The artefact that proves coaching worked is a second set collected because the first one could not support the claim the student wanted to make.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Survey and interview projects should leave a sampling note: who was asked, how many, why those people, and what the sample cannot show. If the only artefact is a results chart, the reflection will have nothing honest to say about validity.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Report drafting lives here. Evidence is a paragraph with a topic sentence that names a decision, journal material quoted and cited, and a visible cut where narration was removed. Successive drafts should get shorter in the retelling and longer in the judgement.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Projects involving a second language, including Arabic as an additional language, produce transcripts, vocabulary logs and recorded attempts. The artefact worth checking is a recording from week one next to one from week eight, which is unusually easy to judge as a parent.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Where a project generates numbers, the evidence is a presentation decision defended: this chart because the data is continuous, this average because the distribution is skewed. A corrected chart with the reason written beside it is one of the clearest single artefacts in the whole project.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Rehearsal logs, annotated drafts, influences compared against the student's own choices. Arts projects generate the most beautiful outcomes and the thinnest records, so the evidence target here is dated process material rather than a better final piece.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Training-plan projects produce the cleanest evidence in the programme: a baseline measurement, a plan, weekly recorded data, and a verdict against the original success criteria. Families who choose this area usually find progress easiest to see week by week.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary work
subjects.description: Projects spanning two subject groups need an explicit note on what each discipline contributed. The missing artefact is nearly always that note, and without it the report reads as two half-projects rather than one integrated piece of work.

subjects.name: Approaches to learning and referencing
subjects.description: Source notes made at the moment of reading, in a consistent format, with what was taken from each one. This is both criterion B evidence and the backbone of the integrity declaration, and it is the artefact most often reconstructed late and least convincing when it is.

regions.note: Apartment living means a quiet room for a video session is the scarce resource, not travel time. Early evening slots work once siblings are settled, and families here often prefer a 30-minute fortnightly check-in over an hour that competes with dinner.

schoolClusters.city: Central and western Dubai IB continuum schools

Outside help should add to that record rather than run a parallel one, so we ask for the school booklet before the first session.

schoolClusters.city: Eastern Dubai and the Mirdif corridor

In that setting the family's own evidence habit carries more weight, because nobody else is checking fortnightly, and a slipped month is only discovered at the deadline.

sections.heading: What a Dubai home tutor for this project would do, and what we do instead
paragraphs: The search term is honest about what families want. A fifteen-year-old building something physical has parts across a table, and a person in the room can pick the thing up. Visiting tutors exist across Dubai and the market rate is published: Bestimate's Dubai survey puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350 per hour, with monthly in-home packages of AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour sessions circulating widely. Those are other providers' figures, read in October 2026, not IB Gram prices.

IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE. Visiting tutors are a service we operate only in India, and saying so on the page is better than taking a booking and explaining afterwards. For every UAE family the format is one-to-one on live video, scheduled to Gulf Standard Time. The case for that is not primarily price, though it usually is cheaper once travel is in the hour. It is that project topics are specific and the pool of adults who have supervised that specific kind of work is not distributed by postcode.

On evidence, which is what this page is about, the comparison is less obvious than it looks and in parts favours video. A visiting tutor sitting beside a student at a laptop tends to end up holding the keyboard, and the artefact that results is a paragraph nobody can confidently attribute. Screen-sharing keeps the document in the student's hands: the coach can point at a sentence and name the strand it fails, and the student types the change. The revision history that comes out of that is both better teaching and better integrity evidence.

sections.heading: The evidence pack: what arrives after a session, and how fast
paragraphs: Every session produces four things, and it is reasonable to demand all four from any provider you pay. A dated note from the coach, short, naming what the student brought and what changed. A journal entry written by the student, ideally during the session. One task for the fortnight, specific enough that a parent can see whether it was done without asking the student to self-report. And, at drafting stage, the annotated draft itself with the student's revisions on top.

The timing matters as much as the content. A note that arrives three days later has already been overtaken. We send it the same evening, which also means it is written while the detail is accurate rather than reconstructed from memory at the end of the week. Parents who read nothing else should read the one-line task, because it is the only part that can be independently verified: either there is a new journal entry about the flow-rate test or there is not.

What a session note should not contain is a character assessment. Comments about a student being bright, engaged or unmotivated tell a parent nothing they did not already know and nothing a school can use. The useful version names the artefact and the criterion: the plan now has revision dates visible, criterion A strand two is evidenced, criterion C still has no verdict against the student's own success criteria. That sentence is checkable. Enthusiasm is not, and a Dubai family comparing two providers will find that the quality of the session note separates them faster than any conversation about qualifications or years of experience does.

sections.heading: What an annotated draft looks like when the student still owns every word
paragraphs: This is the part families most want to see and most rarely get explained. A draft comes back with margin comments, and each comment does one of four jobs. It names a strand the paragraph is meant to evidence and does not. It asks a question the student has to answer in their own words. It points at a sentence that narrates the term rather than judging a decision. Or it flags a citation that needs a source. None of the four supplies replacement text.

A worked example makes the difference concrete. A student writes that they worked hard on the irrigation system and learnt a lot about plants. The unhelpful annotation rewrites it into something fluent. The useful annotation reads: criterion C asks you to judge the product against the success criteria you wrote in September; you set a criterion that the planter would keep soil moisture above a stated level for four days; what happened when you tested it, and what does that tell you about the design choice. The student then writes four sentences that score, in their own voice.

Keeping the draft history is the other half of it. Successive versions are retained so that the trail shows a student's own progression, which is useful teaching feedback and happens to be the cleanest answer available if a school ever asks how the report was produced. Families should be wary of any arrangement where the draft comes back fluent and the student cannot explain a paragraph aloud. That is the failure mode the ghostwriting end of this market produces, and the consequence lands on the student.

sections.heading: Ten weeks of a real Dubai project, week by week
paragraphs: Progress on this component is not smooth, and a log of what actually happens is more useful than a promise. The pattern below is composite rather than one student, drawn from the shape these projects usually take in Dubai schools with a January or February report deadline. It is deliberately unflattering in the middle, because weeks five and six are where most projects stall and where most families assume the coaching has failed.

The useful reading is the right-hand column. Early weeks produce structural artefacts: a goal split, criteria written down, a plan with dates. The middle weeks produce very little, and the coach's job there is to keep the journal alive rather than to force progress that is not available while subject assessment peaks. The late weeks produce drafts, and that is where the earlier structural work either pays for itself or is revealed as absent.

Two things in this log are worth negotiating before you start. First, the mid-project flat spot is normal and should not trigger more sessions. Buying weekly lessons in week six usually adds cost without adding evidence, because the constraint is the student's available hours and not the teaching. Second, the report-drafting weeks need the student present and rested, which in a Dubai term means protecting a slot that mock examinations have not already claimed. A third point is worth raising with the school rather than with us: if your child's report deadline sits inside the mock window, the coordinator may already know that and may have built flexibility into the internal date. Families who ask about that in October occasionally discover a fortnight they did not know they had, and a fortnight at that stage is worth more than four extra paid sessions in December.

sections.heading: Reading progress honestly: what the evidence can and cannot tell you
paragraphs: Parents are offered two bad instruments and one good one. The bad instruments are the child's own mood, which rises after any attentive hour with an adult, and the tutor's enthusiasm, which is a sales signal rather than a measurement. The good instrument is the artefact stack: does it get thicker, and does each item do something the previous one did not. That is a question anyone can answer in ten minutes on a Friday evening without understanding a single criterion.

What the evidence cannot tell you is the final mark. Nobody can forecast a criterion mark on an unsubmitted report, and anyone who offers a predicted band is making it up. School internal moderation applies, standards vary between cohorts, and the conversion from twenty-four raw marks to a reported grade is set by the school. The honest claim is narrower and more useful: this strand had no evidence six weeks ago and now has dated evidence. That is a fact about the work rather than a prophecy about the result.

It also helps to know the realistic horizon. Structural change shows up in a fortnight, because writing two goals apart and three testable criteria is a single session's work. Change in the quality of reflection takes longer, usually around six weeks, because it depends on the student having accumulated decisions worth reflecting on. If nothing has changed in the artefacts after four weeks, that is a genuine signal, and the right response is a conversation about whether the problem is teaching, time or fit, not more sessions.

sections.heading: When the mid-year project grade goes down, and what it usually means
paragraphs: Dubai schools often issue an interim project indication on the mid-year report, and families reasonably panic when it is lower than the autumn comment. In the majority of cases it is not deterioration. It is the first point at which the school has applied the criteria to actual submitted evidence rather than to an intention. An encouraging October comment about a promising topic is not a mark. A January indication against three criteria is, and the drop between them is often the gap between enthusiasm and evidence becoming visible.

The diagnostic question is which criterion moved. A low planning mark at mid-year nearly always means the success criteria were never written in testable form, which is fixable only in the report by being honest about it. A low applying-skills mark means the journal is thin, which can still be improved in the remaining weeks by entries about current decisions. A low reflecting mark at this stage is the least worrying, because reflection is written last and is the part most responsive to coaching.

The response that does not work is adding sessions without changing what they contain. If the mid-year indication is low on planning, more weekly tuition on the product will not move it. The useful move is a single honest session that rewrites the reflection plan: what was intended, what the criteria said, what actually happened, and what the student can now defend. That conversation is uncomfortable and it is the one that converts a mid-band project into a defensible one.

sections.heading: Integrity evidence, and the question that filters this market
paragraphs: The Personal Project carries an academic integrity declaration, signed by the student and countersigned by the school supervisor, stating that the work and thinking are the student's own. Paid coaching does not breach that declaration. Work produced by someone else does. The difference is visible in the artefacts, which is the practical reason an evidence-led arrangement protects a student rather than merely reassuring a parent.

This region has an active market in the wrong direction. Services here advertise finished Internal Assessments at fixed prices, with one found during our research selling completed work at AED 3,750. Buying assessed work is a malpractice matter and the consequence falls on the candidate, not the seller. No Dubai family needs a lecture about this; they need a filter. One question does most of the work: ask what happens if the student does nothing between sessions. A coach says the next session starts by looking at why. A ghostwriting service says it does not matter.

Our own boundary, in writing before any payment: the student writes every word of the report, keeps the journal, makes the product and signs the declaration. A coach questions, reads, names unevidenced strands, explains what a command term requires, models a technique on a different example and checks reference formatting. A coach does not keep the journal, does not supply sentences, does not make the product and does not contact the school. Ask for that list from whoever you hire, and ask for it before the first invoice rather than after.

sections.heading: Stopping: when the evidence says the coaching has done its job
paragraphs: Tutoring arrangements rarely end deliberately, which is how Dubai families end up paying for a weekly slot into May for a project submitted in January. Evidence makes stopping easy to judge. When the journal habit holds without prompting, the report draft is inside the word limit with every strand evidenced, and the student can explain any paragraph aloud, the useful work is finished. Continuing past that point buys reassurance, and reassurance is expensive at specialist hourly rates.

There is one honest exception worth taking, and it is short. A bridge block of two or three sessions immediately after submission converts project habits into Extended Essay habits while the student still remembers what went wrong: how to scope a question, how a reading log differs from a bibliography, how to arrive at a supervisor meeting with something prepared. Dubai students starting DP1 in August gain more from that than from a term of general study-skills sessions a year later.

We would rather tell a family to stop than hold a slot. That is partly principle and partly arithmetic: a family that finishes a project well and returns for Diploma subject support two years later is worth more than four unnecessary invoices, and the Dubai market is small enough that reputation travels between school gates faster than any advertising. If you are reading this with a project already submitted, the sensible next step is the bridge block or nothing at all. If the project has not been submitted and you are unsure which of those two you need, say so when you book the free lesson and the diagnosis will answer it.

sections.heading: The wider UAE context, and what we will not claim about it
paragraphs: Two regulatory facts are worth having straight, because they come up in sales conversations where they should not. Private schools in Dubai are overseen by KHDA, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, per the UAE government's own information service. Abu Dhabi has ADEK, Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority, and the Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. IB Gram holds no permit, accreditation or endorsement from any of them, and nobody should tell you otherwise.

Private tutoring itself is permit-regulated. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and the published service page is Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing on mohre.gov.ae. No fee is listed and no fine schedule is published, so we quote neither.

On the UAE Ministry of Education equivalency question that often follows: the Personal Project is not assessed for equivalency, and no verified IB points threshold exists that we are willing to publish. The British-track requirement is published: five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from the five, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. Verify any figure on moe.gov.ae. Tutoring is not required for equivalency, and a provider suggesting otherwise is manufacturing urgency.

process.title: Send the booklet and the deadline
process.description: The school's project booklet and the submission date tell us more in two minutes than a long conversation about your child. If the booklet names milestone dates, we build the session plan against those rather than against a standard package. No booklet is fine; we will ask the student what the school has said.

process.title: Free 45-minute diagnostic lesson
process.description: One lesson at no cost, no card details, no obligation. It ends with a written diagnosis you keep: the project's current stage, the criterion most at risk, and three things that would change it. Plenty of families take that document and manage the project themselves, which is a fine outcome.

process.title: Match on subject background
process.description: Because delivery is online across the UAE, matching is a question of who has supervised this kind of work rather than who lives nearby. A training-plan project and a short-film project go to different coaches. If nobody suitable is free in the slot you want, we tell you that rather than substituting a generalist.

process.title: Agree the evidence rhythm in writing
process.description: Before any payment you get the session count, their placement against the school's milestones, what each session is for, and what arrives afterwards. No fixed term, no minimum weeks, and blocks can pause for mock examinations or shift to post-Iftar timings during Ramadan.

process.title: Read the note, check the one task
process.description: After each session a dated note arrives the same evening, naming what changed and the single task for the fortnight. Parents who read nothing else should read the task, because it is the only part that can be checked independently: either the entry exists or it does not.

process.title: Review at six weeks, and be willing to stop
process.description: At six weeks we look at the artefact stack together and say plainly whether it is thickening. If it is not, the conversation is about teaching, time or fit rather than about buying more hours. When the work is done we say so, and offer only the short bridge block into DP1.

whyPoints.title: Artefacts, not impressions
whyPoints.description: Every session leaves a dated note, a student-written journal entry and one checkable task. Progress is argued from those documents rather than from how the hour felt, which is the only way a parent can judge a component that is marked once, months away, against criteria they have never read.

whyPoints.title: The document never changes hands
whyPoints.description: Drafts are annotated by strand and returned; the student makes every edit on their own screen. That produces better teaching and a revision history that answers the integrity question before anyone asks it. A fluent draft the student cannot explain aloud is a failure, not a result.

whyPoints.title: Honest about the flat spot
whyPoints.description: Weeks five and six of a Dubai project year are usually empty, because subject assessment peaks there. We say so in advance rather than selling extra sessions into it. The coach's job in those weeks is keeping the journal alive, not manufacturing progress that the timetable does not allow.

whyPoints.title: Subject-aware matching across the UAE
whyPoints.description: Online delivery means the coach is chosen for having supervised this kind of work rather than for living within driving distance of your community. For project topics, which are specific by design, that is the difference between useful questions and general encouragement.

whyPoints.title: We will tell you to stop
whyPoints.description: When the journal habit holds, the draft is complete and the student can defend any paragraph, the useful work is finished. Continuing is reassurance at specialist rates. We would rather end a block early and be the people you call in DP1 than hold a slot nobody needs.

whyPoints.title: No predicted bands, no borrowed authority
whyPoints.description: Nobody can forecast a criterion mark on an unsubmitted report, so we do not. No regulator endorses us, every AED figure on this page belongs to another provider with its source and reading date attached, and every IB detail should be checked against your school's current project guide.

faqs.question: How will I know in week three whether the project coaching is doing anything at all?
faqs.answer: Look at the artefacts rather than at your child's mood. By week three there should be a learning goal and a product goal written as separate sentences, two or three success criteria with a stated test for each, a dated plan, and at least one journal entry in your child's own words. If all four exist, the structural work has happened and that is what week three can realistically deliver. If none exist, that is a genuine signal and worth raising immediately rather than waiting for the mid-year report.

faqs.question: What does a marked report draft actually look like when it comes back?
faqs.answer: Margin comments doing one of four jobs: naming a strand the paragraph fails to evidence, asking a question the student must answer in their own words, pointing at a sentence that narrates rather than judges, or flagging a citation that needs a source. No comment supplies replacement text. The student types every change on their own screen, and successive versions are kept so the revision trail stays visible. If a draft comes back fluent and rewritten, that is a different and much worse product.

faqs.question: My son says sessions are going well but the journal is still empty - what do I ask for?
faqs.answer: Ask for the last three session notes and the one task set at the end of each. Then check whether the tasks produced anything. A session can be pleasant, useful in the room and still leave nothing behind, which usually means the task was too vague to verify. The fix is narrower tasks: not keep working on the journal, but write a dated entry about why the second prototype leaked. Ask the coach to set the task in that form from now on.

faqs.question: Can you show me a criterion mark going up, or is that not how this component works?
faqs.answer: Not in the way a past-paper score goes up, and any provider promising otherwise is overselling. The report is marked once, by the school, with internal moderation, and the conversion from twenty-four raw marks to a reported grade is set locally. What we can show is narrower and real: a strand that had no evidence six weeks ago now has dated evidence, and a paragraph that narrated the term now judges a decision against a criterion the student wrote. That is a fact about the work rather than a forecast.

faqs.question: What do you send after each session, and will I get to read my child's draft?
faqs.answer: A dated note the same evening, naming what the student brought, which strand the session addressed, and one task for the fortnight. At drafting stage the annotated draft follows within 48 hours. Whether you read the draft is your child's call as much as ours, and we would encourage you to ask rather than require. Fifteen-year-olds who feel the work is surveilled tend to write for the audience, which makes the reflection worse. The session notes give you the picture without taking the project off them.

faqs.question: How many weeks before the school supervisor sees a difference in my child?
faqs.answer: Usually by the second supervisor meeting after sessions start, which in most Dubai schools is four to eight weeks. The change supervisors notice first is not better work, it is better preparation: a student arriving with a journal, two specific questions and a decision to defend rather than an apology. That shift happens quickly because it is a habit rather than a skill, and it tends to make supervisors more generous with their time, which has its own compounding effect.

faqs.question: My daughter's mid-year project indication dropped - has the coaching failed?
faqs.answer: Probably not. A mid-year indication is often the first point at which the school applies the three criteria to submitted evidence rather than to an intention, so the drop is frequently the gap between enthusiasm and evidence becoming visible. Ask which criterion moved. A low planning mark means the success criteria were never testable and must now be handled honestly in the reflection. A low applying-skills mark means a thin journal, which current entries can still improve. A low reflecting mark this early is the least concerning.

faqs.question: Who decides when project coaching should stop, and will you tell me?
faqs.answer: We will tell you. The conditions are specific: the journal habit holds without prompting, the draft sits inside the word limit with every strand evidenced, and the student can explain any paragraph aloud without reading it. At that point continuing buys reassurance at specialist hourly rates. The only short extension worth taking is a two or three session bridge block immediately after submission for students continuing into DP1, which converts project habits into Extended Essay habits while they are fresh.

faqs.question: Do you contact my child's school supervisor about the project?
faqs.answer: No. The supervisor relationship belongs to the student, the school owns the project process, and the supervisor countersigns the integrity declaration. Our role is to prepare the student to arrive at those meetings with a journal, questions and a decision to defend. If a school asks a family how outside support was used, the honest answer is easy to give because the artefacts show it: annotated drafts with the student's own revisions, and journal entries in the student's own voice.

faqs.question: Is there any point hiring someone to sit beside my child while the report gets written?
faqs.answer: It is the format with the highest risk of the wrong outcome. A tutor beside a student at a laptop tends to end up holding the keyboard, and what results is a paragraph nobody can confidently attribute. Screen-sharing keeps the document in the student's hands: the coach points at a sentence and names the strand, the student types the change. That produces a revision history which is both better feedback and the cleanest possible answer to the integrity question.

faqs.question: Does a visiting tutor in Dubai produce better evidence than a video session?
faqs.answer: On one thing, yes: looking at a physical product in the room is genuinely better, and that is worth saying. On everything else the comparison favours video, because the journal, the plan, the referencing and the report are all screen work. A visiting session typically leaves a verbal summary at the door; a video session leaves a dated written note the same evening. IB Gram does not run home visits in Dubai in any case, so for us the honest comparison is between video and the market's in-home rate of AED 180 to 350 per hour.

faqs.question: What evidence should I ask any Dubai project tutor for before the second payment?
faqs.answer: Four things, all reasonable and all cheap to supply. The session notes so far, with dates. The task set at the end of each session and whether it was done. One annotated draft, so you can see whether feedback names strands or supplies sentences. And the provider's written boundary list: what they will and will not do with the journal, the product and the report. A provider who cannot produce those four after three sessions is selling time rather than teaching.

faqs.question: My child refuses to let anyone read the process journal - how should we handle that?
faqs.answer: Treat it as reasonable and work around it rather than through it. The journal is the student's own record and some fifteen-year-olds write far more honestly when they know a parent is not reading it. The workable compromise is that the coach reads it in session, the student chooses which entries to show at home, and the parent gets the dated session note instead. The non-negotiable part is that entries exist and are dated, because the integrity declaration and criterion B both depend on it.

faqs.question: Can two children in different MYP years share a coach and still get separate evidence?
faqs.answer: They can share a coach, and some families prefer the continuity, but they should not share a session. A joint hour produces one note and a blurred picture of who did what, which defeats the purpose of evidence-led support and is unhelpful if a school later asks about outside help. Two separate thirty-minute slots cost the same as one hour at most providers and produce two distinct artefact trails. For households in areas like Al Qusais with several children in different programmes, that split matters.

faqs.question: What does the free first lesson leave me with if we decide not to continue?
faqs.answer: A written diagnosis you keep: the stage the project is genuinely at, which of the three criteria is most at risk, and three specific actions that would change it. No card details are taken and nothing follows automatically. A meaningful number of Dubai families take that document, work through it themselves with the school supervisor, and never book a paid session. That is a legitimate outcome and we would rather be useful once than sell a block nobody needed.

faqs.question: The product is already finished - is there any evidence left to build?
faqs.answer: Yes, and more than families expect. A finished product can still be tested against the success criteria, which produces a dated record that feeds two criteria. The journal can carry honest entries about the remaining weeks, including the reconstruction being acknowledged as reconstruction. And the report, which is where most of the marks sit, has not been written yet. What cannot be manufactured is six months of decision-making, so the reflection has to be honest about that, and honesty there scores better than families fear.

The answers will separate them faster than any conversation about experience. Our free 45-minute first lesson ends with a written diagnosis of the project's real stage and the criterion most at risk, taken with no card details and no obligation. Lessons run one-to-one on live video across the UAE, timed to Gulf Standard Time, and your child writes every word that carries their name on it.

dubai/ib-myp-personal-project-tutor.tutorsIntro: The coaches below work on MYP 5 projects: process journals, learning and product goals, criterion-referenced report drafts, and the supervisor conversation your child has to lead. Each holds a subject background, because a project about water reuse and a project about a short film need different questions asked of them.

intro.heading: The Personal Project is marked on process, and the process is where Dubai students lose it
paragraphs: Parents usually come to this page because a product is finished and a report is not. The model aeroplane flies, the recipe book is printed, the fundraiser raised money, and the folder of written work that the IB actually marks is three paragraphs long and due in eleven days. That is the normal shape of the problem. The Personal Project does not give marks for how impressive the outcome is. It gives marks for whether the student can show how they planned it, which skills they chose and applied, and what they can now say honestly about the gap between what they intended and what they produced.

That gap between effort and mark is what an IB MYP Personal Project tutor in Dubai is hired to close. The project is assessed against three criteria, each marked from 0 to 8, and the strands inside each criterion are specific about the evidence they expect. A student who built something genuinely good can still land in the middle band because the journal is thin, the success criteria were never written down, and the reflection describes feelings rather than decisions. None of that is a lack of ability. It is a reporting problem, and reporting is teachable in a way that inspiration is not.

Dubai adds its own pressure. The emirate had 227 private schools and 387,441 pupils in 2024-25, offering 17 different curricula, with IB programmes accounting for around 7% of the private-school roll, according to the Dubai Media Office. That means MYP 5 cohorts here are small relative to the British-curriculum majority, and a school may run one Personal Project coordinator across a year group with wide-ranging topics. Supervisors are generous but stretched. A student whose project sits outside their supervisor's subject area often gets encouragement rather than the sharper, more awkward questions that move a criterion mark.

The second Dubai pressure is the calendar. Schools set their own Personal Project deadlines, and in this emirate the internal submission date commonly lands between December and February of MYP 5, well before the Diploma option sheets go out and in the same term as school-level mock examinations. Families who start project support in the final fortnight are buying editing. Families who start in September are buying structure, which is the thing the criteria reward. Add Ramadan, which moves evening availability for part of the spring term, and the planning question becomes concrete rather than theoretical.

What follows is the page we would want if our own child were in MYP 5 at a Dubai IB school: what the three criteria ask for strand by strand, how a learning goal differs from a product goal, what belongs in a process journal and how often, the deadline counted backwards, where in Dubai a product can realistically be made, and exactly where a private tutor has to stop. Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. Nothing on this page is a promise about a grade.

dubai/ib-myp-personal-project-tutor.programmesIntro: The Personal Project sits at the end of a five-year programme, and what came before it decides how hard the final year is. These are the stages IB Gram covers for Dubai families, with what each one means locally.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme, early years
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each reported against four criteria marked 0 to 8 rather than percentages. This is where approaches-to-learning skills are supposed to be built: research questioning, source evaluation, time planning, self-management. Students who arrive at the Personal Project unable to keep a dated record of their own thinking are usually students for whom these three years were graded but never explicitly taught as skills.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai, many IB continuum schools take a large intake at Year 7 from British-curriculum primaries nearby. Those pupils meet criterion-referenced marking for the first time, and the habit of writing down a plan before starting work is the single transferable thing that pays off four years later in the Personal Project.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme, final two years
programmes.description: Subject work deepens, mathematics splits into standard and extended routes, and in the final year the Personal Project runs alongside everything else. Some Dubai schools also enter candidates for end-of-programme eAssessment. The workload clash is real: the project needs sustained independent time in the same months that subject teachers are setting summative tasks.
programmes.countryNote: A Dubai MYP 5 student is often making two decisions at once: the Personal Project topic, and whether to continue into the Diploma or move to a school running A Level. Several Dubai schools require the project to be submitted before Diploma subject choices are confirmed, which is why September planning beats January rescue work.

programmes.name: The Personal Project itself
programmes.description: An independent piece of work with a learning goal, a product or outcome, a process journal kept throughout, and a report submitted against three criteria. A supervisor from the school meets the student periodically. The student signs an academic integrity form confirming the work and the thinking behind it are their own.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools vary widely in how much structure they wrap around this. Some run timetabled project lessons and a fixed milestone schedule; others hand out a booklet in September and expect the student to manage. Knowing which kind of school your child is in changes what outside support is for.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at higher level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and creativity, activity, service. Every subject carries an internal assessment. The research habits the Personal Project is meant to install are the same ones the Extended Essay assumes are already there, which is why a weak project year tends to show up again eighteen months later.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai has a large Diploma cohort spread across both continuum schools and schools that offer only the final two years. A student arriving into DP1 from a Dubai MYP 5 where the project was treated as a box to tick typically needs the research-question discipline rebuilt from scratch in the first Extended Essay term.

dubai/ib-myp-personal-project-tutor.subjectsIntro: A Personal Project grows out of a subject interest, and the coach needs to be able to ask subject questions. These are the areas Dubai families most often ask us to pair with the project, with what each one contributes to the evidence.

subjects.name: Design and product development
subjects.description: Design-rooted projects live or die on recorded iteration. A coach pushes for sketched alternatives, specification criteria written before building, and a tested prototype with a dated record of what failed. That record is what feeds the applying-skills criterion far more reliably than a polished final object.

subjects.name: Sciences and investigation design
subjects.description: Projects involving measurement, growth experiments, water quality or air readings need a control, a repeat and an honest error discussion. Dubai students often choose a science question and then collect one set of numbers. The coaching work is turning a single data capture into a defensible method.

subjects.name: Individuals and societies research
subjects.description: Survey and interview projects raise consent and sampling issues that MYP 5 students rarely anticipate. Who did you ask, how many, and why those people. A coach helps design something answerable in the time available rather than a questionnaire sent to a family WhatsApp group.

subjects.name: Language and literature: report writing
subjects.description: The report is a piece of structured non-fiction with a job to do. Paragraphs must evidence a strand, not narrate a term. Sessions work on topic sentences that name the decision, appropriate use of the student's own journal as cited evidence, and cutting the retelling that eats the word count.

subjects.name: Arts: process documentation
subjects.description: Visual art, music and drama outcomes are the easiest to over-invest in and the hardest to evidence. Photographs of a finished piece prove little. Rehearsal logs, annotated drafts, influences compared against the student's own choices and dated revisions are what the criteria can actually reward.

subjects.name: Mathematics and data handling
subjects.description: Where a project generates numbers, presentation decisions matter: which chart, which average, what the sample size permits. Students frequently use a pie chart where the data is continuous, then draw a conclusion the figures cannot support. Fixing this takes one session and usually moves the reflection quality too.

subjects.name: Approaches to learning: research skills
subjects.description: Source selection, note-taking that survives a month, referencing in a consistent style, and distinguishing a claim from evidence. These are named skills in the programme and they are the ones most often assumed rather than taught. They are also directly cite-able in the report.

subjects.name: Approaches to learning: self-management
subjects.description: Breaking a six-month project into fortnightly deliverables, keeping a dated journal, and preparing for a supervisor meeting with questions rather than apologies. For a Dubai student juggling a project, mock examinations and mandatory UAE subjects, this is the skill that decides whether the work exists at all.

subjects.name: Academic integrity and referencing
subjects.description: What counts as help, what must be attributed, and how to record where an idea came from at the moment it arrives rather than reconstructing it later. The integrity form the student signs is specific, and students who have kept a referenced journal sign it without anxiety.

subjects.name: Arabic, Islamic Education and UAE Social Studies
subjects.description: These subjects are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, per KHDA's mandatory-subjects guidelines. They occupy timetable space in the same year as the Personal Project, and families planning project time need to count them rather than discover them in February.

dubai/ib-myp-personal-project-tutor.regionsTitle: Where a Dubai Personal Project can actually get made
dubai/ib-myp-personal-project-tutor.regionsIntro: Product goals fail for logistical reasons more often than intellectual ones. A project needs a workshop, a site, an archive or a willing expert within reach of a school evening. These are the parts of Dubai that make particular products possible, and what to plan around in each.

regions.name: Al Quoz and Alserkal Avenue
regions.note: Dubai's fabrication and gallery district. Makerspaces, print shops, upholsterers and metal workshops sit within a few streets, which makes a physical product realistic for a student who can get there once. Access needs an adult and a weekend slot; nothing here runs on a Tuesday evening.

regions.name: Dubai Design District and Business Bay
regions.note: Studios, architecture practices and brand agencies cluster here, and a short interview with a working designer is a legitimate research source if it is recorded and cited. Students should ask by email, with a named question list, not a general request for help.

regions.name: Ras Al Khor and the Dubai Creek wetlands
regions.note: A protected flamingo and mangrove site with public hides. Environmental projects can gather observational data here across repeat visits, which is what turns a nature interest into a method. Visits are early morning and seasonal; the plan has to account for summer heat.

regions.name: Mushrif Park and Al Warqa
regions.note: Mature woodland and open ground within reach of eastern Dubai schools, useful for soil, shade, litter-survey and biodiversity counts that need the same spot sampled more than once. Families in Mirdif and Al Warqa can treat it as a repeatable site rather than a one-off trip.

regions.name: Dubai Internet City and Dubai Silicon Oasis
regions.note: Where a student building software or hardware can find a mentor who will answer a specific technical question. Parents working in these free zones are the most underused resource in the whole project: a colleague's half-hour is worth more than a week of tutorials.

regions.name: Jumeirah, Al Safa and Umm Suqeim
regions.note: Beach-front projects on plastics, shoreline litter or water clarity are popular here and genuinely repeatable, since the same transect can be walked weekly. The common failure is one spectacular beach-clean photograph and no comparative measurement.

regions.name: Emirates Hills, Al Barsha South and Dubai Hills
regions.note: Dense in IB continuum schools, so cohorts here often choose similar topics in the same year. Supervisors notice. A project with a local, specific question tends to get a sharper supervisor conversation than a broad global topic chosen from a list.

regions.name: Dubai Investments Park and Green Community
regions.note: Light-industrial neighbours, nurseries and plant suppliers make agricultural and horticultural products practical, including growth trials that need two months. Travel time from central Dubai is the constraint, so the site visit schedule has to be fixed in September.

schoolClusters.city: Emirates Hills, Al Barsha and Dubai Hills
schoolClusters.note: The densest cluster of IB continuum schools in the emirate, which means a concentration of MYP 5 cohorts reaching the Personal Project in the same term. Students we support here most often need help narrowing a topic that is too large, and holding one line of inquiry across a term with heavy subject assessment.

schoolClusters.city: Mirdif, Dubai Investments Park and the eastern corridor
schoolClusters.note: IB continuum provision spread across a wider area, with longer school runs and project time competing with travel. Students we support from these communities often choose products that can be made at home or on a single weekend site visit, which is a sensible constraint rather than a compromise.

modes.description: Three or four sessions in the first weeks: choosing a learning goal that can be evidenced, separating it from the product goal, writing success criteria before anything is built, and setting up a journal that will survive six months. This block is the one that changes the final mark most and is the one families most often skip.

modes.description: A short recurring session that exists to keep the record honest. The student brings the journal, talks through what moved and what stalled, and leaves with one concrete action. This is deliberately lighter than weekly subject tutoring, because the project needs independent time more than it needs instruction.

sections.heading: What a Personal Project tutor in Dubai is actually hired to fix
paragraphs: An IB MYP Personal Project tutor in Dubai is hired for one of four situations, and it is worth knowing which one you are in before buying anything. The first is a student with no topic in October. The second is a student with a topic, a product half-built, and no written record of any decision made so far. The third is a student with a finished product and a report that reads like a diary. The fourth, less common and more serious, is a student whose project has drifted so far from the original learning goal that the report cannot honestly claim the two are connected.

Each needs a different first session. The student with no topic needs questions, not suggestions: what have you fixed, built, organised or argued about in the last two years, and what did you not finish. The student with no record needs a reconstruction that is honest about being a reconstruction, plus a journal habit that holds for the remaining months. The student with a diary-style report needs the criteria read aloud, strand by strand, against their own paragraphs. The student who has drifted needs the hardest conversation: either reframe the learning goal to match what was really learned, or state the divergence openly in the reflection, which the criteria can reward.

What a coach does not do is take the project over. The product belongs to the student, the journal is the student's own record, and every word of the report is written by the student. That boundary is not a marketing position, it is the condition of the qualification. A project that a tutor has effectively produced is worthless at best and a malpractice matter at worst. Our sessions are built so the student leaves with a task, and the next session starts by looking at whether they did it.
bullets: No topic yet: the session is a structured interview, not a list of ideas
No journal: reconstruct honestly, then build a habit that survives six months
Diary-style report: read the strands against the student's own paragraphs
Drifted project: reframe the goal or declare the divergence in the reflection

sections.heading: The three criteria, strand by strand, and what each mark actually asks
paragraphs: The Personal Project is assessed against three criteria, each marked from 0 to 8, giving a total out of 24 that the school converts into a reported grade. Confirm the current criterion letters, strand wording and conversion bands with your child's MYP coordinator, because the project guide has been revised and schools apply the current version. What does not change is the logic: each criterion has named strands, and a mark in a band requires evidence of every strand in that band, not an average impression of effort.

Criterion A covers planning. Its strands ask the student to state a learning goal and a product goal, define success criteria for the product, and present a plan with evidence that it was followed or adapted. The common Dubai failure here is a success criterion that cannot be checked, such as the product being enjoyable. A checkable criterion names the test: the recipe book is usable by someone who has not cooked before, verified by two people cooking from it unaided.

Criterion B covers applying skills. Its strands ask which approaches-to-learning skills the student used and how, and how subject knowledge and understanding were applied. This is where a thin journal costs the most, because the criterion rewards demonstrated application rather than claimed effort. Criterion C covers reflecting: on the quality of the product against the success criteria, on what was learned about the topic and about themselves as a learner. Honest reflection on a partial failure routinely scores higher than a cheerful account of a success, and students find that genuinely hard to believe until they see it marked.

sections.heading: A learning goal is not a product goal, and conflating them costs marks all year
paragraphs: Almost every weak project we see in Dubai starts with one sentence doing two jobs. A student writes that they want to build a working hydroponic planter, and treats that as the whole goal. It is a product goal. The learning goal is the separate question of what the student intends to get better at or come to understand: nutrient chemistry, irrigation control, or how to design for a climate where water evaporates faster than plants can use it. The criteria assess both, and the reflection at the end has to judge each against its own standard.

Written apart, the two goals make the whole year easier. The product goal tells you what to build and when it is finished. The learning goal tells you what to record while building it, which is precisely the material that feeds criterion B. A student who knows their learning goal is irrigation control writes journal entries about flow rate experiments. A student who thinks the goal is the planter writes entries about trips to buy fittings. The first set evidences a strand; the second set evidences shopping.

This is also how a drifting project gets saved. Products fail for ordinary reasons: a part does not arrive, a venue says no, a school term swallows three weeks. If the learning goal was stated separately and clearly, the student can report honestly that the product fell short while the learning happened, and criterion C can reward that account. If the two were fused into one sentence in September, a failed product reads as a failed project, and the report ends up arguing against the evidence. We spend a full session on this split with every Dubai student in the planning block, and it is the single cheapest intervention on offer.
bullets: Product goal: what will exist at the end, and the test that says it is finished
Learning goal: what the student will understand or be able to do that they could not before
Journal entries should serve the learning goal, not narrate the shopping
Separating them is what lets an honest report survive a product that underperformed

sections.heading: The process journal: the part nobody else can keep for your child
paragraphs: The process journal is the spine of the assessment. It is the student's own working record, kept while the work happens, and it is the only place the evidence for criterion B can come from. Schools differ on format: a notebook, a shared document, a slide deck, a folder of photographs with captions. What matters is that entries are dated, specific and written at the time. A journal assembled the week before submission is visible to any experienced reader, and it undermines the integrity form the student has to sign.

A good entry is short and decision-shaped. It names what was attempted, what happened, what the student decided to do next, and why. Four sentences is plenty. Students in Dubai tend to either write nothing for six weeks or produce long reflective essays that exhaust them by October. Neither works. A fortnightly four-sentence entry across the project year gives the report roughly fifteen dated decisions to cite, which is more than enough for a strong criterion B case.

The coaching role here is narrow by design. A tutor can ask what the student did last fortnight, point out that an entry records an action without a reason, and show how a journal extract becomes a cited sentence in the report. A tutor cannot keep the journal, dictate entries or supply the reasoning. We ask the student to write the entry during the session while the thinking is live, then read it back. That takes ten minutes and produces something the student can defend in a supervisor meeting.

sections.heading: The internal deadline, counted backwards from your school's own date
paragraphs: Dubai schools set their own Personal Project milestones, and the only date that matters to your family is the one in your child's project booklet. The IB does not publish a global submission date for this component, so anyone quoting you one is guessing. What is predictable is the shape: topic approval early in the autumn term, a supervisor meeting schedule, a product completion point, then a report submission some weeks later, with the school's internal moderation after that. In this emirate the report deadline commonly falls between December and February of MYP 5.

Counted backwards, that date is less frightening than it looks. If the report is due in late January, the product needs to be finished and tested by the start of January, which means the last build phase runs through November, which means success criteria and a plan must exist in late September. Working forwards, families consistently underestimate the gap between a product being finished and a report being ready. Two to three weeks is realistic for a student writing 1,500 to 3,500 words of criterion-referenced prose from a journal they already keep. Without a journal, the same task takes a month and produces weaker evidence.

The two Dubai-specific collisions to put in the calendar early are school mock examinations, which in many schools sit in the same window as the project deadline, and Ramadan, which shortens school days and shifts family evenings for part of the spring term. If your child's deadline falls after Ramadan begins, the serious project work has to be done before it, not during. We plan sessions around both as a matter of course, including moving slots to post-Iftar timing where a family prefers that.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: the integrity form, the supervisor, and where a private coach stops
paragraphs: The Personal Project carries an academic integrity form that the student signs and the supervisor countersigns. It is a statement that the work, and the thinking behind it, belong to the student. Paid help is not forbidden by that statement, and plenty of Dubai families use a coach, a tutor or a specialist mentor. What is forbidden is help that displaces the student's own work or thinking. The distinction is not subtle in practice, and it is worth being explicit with your child about it before anyone is hired.

There is an active market in this SERP for exactly the wrong thing. Services in this region advertise finished Internal Assessments at fixed prices. Buying assessed work is a malpractice matter for the student, and the consequence lands on the student, not the seller. A Dubai family can check a provider in one question: ask what happens if the student does not do the homework between sessions. A coach will say the next session reviews why. A ghostwriting service will say it does not matter.

Our own boundary, stated plainly: a coach may ask questions, read the student's draft and name which strand a paragraph fails to evidence, explain what a command term requires, model a technique on a different example, and check that a reference is formatted correctly. A coach does not supply the topic as a finished package, does not write or redraft any part of the report, does not keep the journal, does not make the product, and does not speak to the school on the student's behalf. Those are not policy flourishes; they are the line that keeps the qualification worth having.

sections.heading: What Personal Project support costs in Dubai, and how blocks are usually bought
paragraphs: Published tutoring rates in Dubai are easy to find and rarely explained, so here is the market as it stood when we read it in October 2026. EdFlik advertises online tuition from AED 45 to AED 65 per hour and Tutopiya from roughly AED 33 to AED 52, both at the budget end using less experienced tutors. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB tuition from AED 200. TutorChase lists AED 270 per hour for specialist IB support. Bestimate's Dubai rate survey puts in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to AED 350, and specialist exam-year help at AED 200 to AED 450 and above. BartyED quotes AED 650 for premium named tutors. Those are other providers' figures, published by them, read on the dates above, not IB Gram prices.

Project support behaves differently from weekly subject tutoring, because the work is lumpy. Most Dubai families who handle it well buy two or three blocks rather than a standing weekly slot: a planning block in the autumn, light fortnightly check-ins through the build, and a report clinic in the final weeks. Bought that way, total hours across the whole project year often come in below a single term of weekly subject tuition, because the sessions are placed where they change the evidence rather than spread evenly for comfort.

The table below does the arithmetic on the mid-market band so you can sanity-check any quote, including ours. IB Gram does not publish a fixed hourly price on these pages, because the right coach for a Design project and the right coach for a sociology survey are different people with different experience. What we do publish is the structure, a free first lesson of 45 minutes with no card details required, and the fact that there is no fixed-term commitment. Ask any provider for the same three things in writing.

sections.heading: Home tutoring for a Dubai project, honestly compared with one-to-one online
paragraphs: Many Dubai parents search for a tutor who will come to the villa, and the reasoning is sound: a fourteen-year-old working on a physical product has materials spread across a table, and a person in the room can look at the thing. That is a real advantage and it is worth saying so. The market exists, Bestimate's survey puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350 per hour, and monthly in-home packages of AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour sessions circulate widely in this emirate.

IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE. Visiting tutors are a service we run only in India, and we would rather say that on the page than take a booking and explain later. For Dubai families, every lesson is one-to-one on live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. The honest case for that is not cost, although it usually is cheaper. It is the tutor pool. A Personal Project on textile dyeing, aquaponics or Arduino sensing needs someone who has supervised that kind of work, and the chance that such a person lives within a twenty-minute drive of Mirdif on a Tuesday at six is small.

There is also a practical point about the project specifically. The journal, the plan, the report and the referencing are all screen work. Screen-sharing a draft and marking which strand a paragraph fails to evidence is genuinely better on video than over a shoulder, because the student keeps control of the document and the revision happens in their own hands. For the parts that need physical presence, a phone camera on a workbench covers more than parents expect. The table sets out the trade honestly, including where in-home wins.

sections.heading: What the project is worth afterwards: the MYP certificate, the Diploma, and the UAE context
paragraphs: Parents reasonably ask what the Personal Project buys. Inside the programme, a satisfactory project is part of what the IB requires for the MYP certificate at schools that register for it, alongside subject results and the end-of-programme eAssessment where a school enters candidates. Many Dubai schools do not register for the certificate at all and simply report the project grade on the school transcript. Ask your child's coordinator which applies, because it changes nothing about the work but quite a lot about how the result is used.

Outside the programme, the project is not a qualification the UAE Ministry of Education assesses for equivalency. Equivalency rules are set by the Ministry and are specific about what each curriculum must show. For the British track, the published requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not counted among the five, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. No IB points threshold has been published that we can verify, so we do not quote one; check moe.gov.ae or the emirate attestation authority before planning around any figure. Tutoring is not required for equivalency and nobody should tell you it is.

The honest answer about value is about the next two years. The Extended Essay in the Diploma assumes a student can hold a question for months, keep a reading record, meet a supervisor with something prepared, and write a self-critical account at the end. Those are the Personal Project's habits exactly. The Dubai students who find DP1 hardest are rarely the ones who lacked content knowledge; they are the ones for whom the project was a weekend of panic in January. That is the real reason to take it seriously, and the reason the planning block is worth more than the rescue.
